Even so, the course carries a GT-AH1 general-studies designation, tying it to Colorado's statutory gtPathways transfer core. That institutional mandate is the binding constraint at this horizon: it requires an arts-and-humanities history offering like this one regardless of how capably AI can already draft a rock-history essay, holding the near-term rating to the low band.

By 2031, AI research and writing tools should competently draft narrative history of Rock and Roll's artists, commercial forces, and cultural controversies, and observed-usage data already shows writing and office-style tasks are a prominent category of real AI use. Verification burden for a survey-style history course is moderate rather than low, factual errors and misattributed cultural claims are plausible but not high-stakes in the way clinical or legal errors are, so this course does not receive the extra dampening some higher-stakes fields get. What still anchors the rating is the GT-AH1 gtPathways designation, a transfer-core mandate structurally independent of task automatability. That combination, rising task exposure, moderate verification burden, but a persistent institutional requirement, produces a medium rather than high rating, with genuine uncertainty about how fast history-survey pedagogy itself might change.

A ten-year horizon invites real hedging: METR and Epoch capability trend research suggests AI task competence keeps compounding, but Census BTOS diffusion data show firm-level AI adoption lagging capability considerably even in fast-moving domains, and classroom practice often lags workplace practice further still. If AI can eventually synthesize the same race-politics-gender-capitalism narrative this course builds toward with near-expert polish, the underlying instrumental need for a human-taught survey narrows. But the GT-AH1 gtPathways transfer-core designation is not capability-contingent: it is a statutory requirement that this kind of arts-and-humanities course exist in the curriculum for transfer students, and nothing about AI competence changes that mandate directly. The rating therefore holds at medium a decade out, anchored by course designation rather than by any judgment about AI's ultimate ceiling.
MUS 1050.d: In this course, students survey the origins and history of Rock and Roll. In addition to examining the songs and influence of significant artists, students explore how the issues of race, politics, gender, and the forces of capitalism have shaped this tradition and subsequently popular culture in America.

r: This course teaches modern production technique across Digital Audio Workstations and video-editing software, having students create and collaborate on digital audio and video productions. These are exactly the interacting-with-computers, content-production tasks where observed AI usage concentrates: Anthropic Economic Index data shows Computer and Mathematical work as the largest usage category, and productivity research on tools like GitHub Copilot documents large task-speed gains in comparable software-driven creative work. AI-assisted mixing, mastering, and video-editing features are already appearing inside mainstream DAWs and editing suites, directly overlapping this course's hands-on practice. No general-studies designation applies, and the course is a standalone two-credit elective rather than a prerequisite for further required coursework, so no institutional or foundational brake tempers this near-term rating, producing a moderate rating today, ahead of most gen-ed music courses.

By 2031, AI-assisted production features, automated mixing suggestions, stem separation, adaptive scoring, video-cut assembly, are plausible to be standard rather than novel inside the DAWs and editing platforms this course already uses. Productivity RCT evidence on comparable software-assisted creative work shows large speed gains, particularly benefiting less experienced users, which mirrors this course's role introducing production techniques to non-specialists. Verification burden stays moderate: students still need to judge whether an AI-suggested mix or edit serves their creative intent, but the stakes of a basic-production elective are low enough that expert oversight is not essential. With no general-studies designation and no foundational role feeding advanced required coursework, nothing structurally protects this course from rising task exposure, pushing the rating to high at this horizon.

Ten years out, firm predictions about specific production tools are unwise, but the direction is consistent: capability trend data from METR and Epoch describe task-time-horizons for AI systems compounding rapidly, and production tasks, arranging, mixing, basic video assembly, are narrow and digitally native compared to work requiring physical presence or adversarial judgment. Diffusion research is the main check on this trajectory: Census BTOS figures show a modest share of firms actually using AI tools even recently, meaning classroom and industry practice may lag raw capability by years. This course carries no general-studies designation and is not a gateway to further required coursework, so no institutional lock-in restrains the rating regardless of adoption pace. The rating stays high at this horizon, reflecting strong underlying task exposure tempered only by uncertainty about how quickly practice actually changes.
MUS 1060.d: This course provides students with a survey of modern music production techniques, devices, platforms, artists and repertoire. Students work, create, and collaborate in the world of digital music and incorporate digital video technology into audio productions. The course involves hands on practice using Digital Audio Workstations (DAWs) and video editing software.

r: This course delivers individual private instruction in performance skills and technique to any student with prior music experience, gated by instructor permission. The work is a real-time, embodied teacher-student exchange, listening to tone, breath support, fingering, or intonation and giving immediate corrective feedback, the kind of psychomotor, in-person coaching that task-exposure research treats as comparatively low-exposure relative to writing or data-processing work. Verification burden is also protective here: judging whether a student's tone or technique has actually improved requires a human ear embedded in the interaction, not a document to be checked afterward. Embodiment and presence are similarly low, since the entire value of the course is synchronous physical demonstration and correction. No general-studies designation or foundational role affects the rating; the constraint is intrinsic to the activity itself, holding this course to a low rating today.

By 2031, AI practice-companion apps may offer decent pitch and rhythm feedback for solo practice between lessons, and some of that augmentation is already visible in observed AI usage patterns skewing toward assistive rather than fully autonomous tasks. But jagged-frontier research is instructive here: AI performs markedly worse once pushed outside a well-defined competence zone, and real-time embodied coaching, reading a student's posture, breath, and instrument-specific technique, sits well outside current systems' zone of reliable competence. The verification burden and embodiment dampeners both remain active at this horizon: technique correction still needs an expert physically present with the student. Private instruction's low exposure rating should hold, with only the possibility that AI tools supplement rather than substitute for the instructor's role between formal sessions.

A ten-year horizon warrants strong hedging for embodied instruction specifically, since capability trends documented by METR and Epoch describe rapid gains in digital, text-based task competence but say much less about real-time physical coaching. Even generous extrapolation of AI's growing task-time-horizon does not obviously transfer to synchronous correction of embouchure, bowing, or vocal technique, which depends on physical presence and immediate multisensory judgment. Diffusion evidence further suggests that even where AI capability advances, adoption in intimate, relationship-based teaching contexts like private lessons could lag other domains considerably. Both the embodiment and verification-burden dampeners are structural rather than merely current-technology limitations, since they concern the nature of the coaching interaction itself. The rating stays low at this horizon, acknowledging uncertainty about hybrid practice-plus-AI models while doubting full substitution for individualized instruction.
MUS 1071.d: This course covers individual private instruction for students of any major with previous music experience to continue to learn performance skills and techniques.

r: Music Theory I develops the ability to analyze and compose diatonic music, Roman numeral and lead-sheet analysis, phrase structure, aural and visual recognition, skills central to classical, jazz, and popular styles. These are structured, rule-governed cognitive tasks similar to the kind of pattern-based reasoning AI already handles competently; observed AI usage data shows Computer and Mathematical work dominating consumer and API use, and harmonic analysis has a comparably formal, notation-based structure. Even so, the binding constraint on this course is foundational rather than institutional: it is a required prerequisite substrate that Music Theory II, its paired lab, and the broader theory sequence for majors all depend on directly. That prerequisite role caps the rating at medium regardless of how automatable individual analysis tasks become, because the course's function in the curriculum is not itself substitutable by a standalone AI tool.

By 2031, AI tools should competently perform much of the mechanical analytical work this course teaches, labeling chords, identifying non-chord tones, generating practice exercises, since capability trend research describes AI task-time-horizons compounding every few months. Verification burden stays moderate: theory homework has checkable right answers, but building genuine fluency in harmonic reasoning still benefits from instructor feedback on partially-correct or ambiguous student work. The course's foundational role remains the dominant constraint at this horizon. Because Music Theory II and its lab, along with later required coursework, structurally depend on the vocabulary and skills built here, no degree of AI capability in performing analysis tasks removes the instrumental need for students to pass through this specific course. The rating holds at medium, reflecting rising task exposure fully offset by curricular sequencing.

Ten years out, confident prediction about AI's ceiling on music-theoretic reasoning is unwarranted, though the general capability trajectory described by METR and Epoch points toward AI systems handling increasingly long and complex analytical tasks. Whatever that ceiling turns out to be, the foundational-scaffolding constraint on this course is structural rather than capability-contingent: as long as MSU Denver's theory sequence requires this course before Theory II and its lab, the instrumental need to take it persists independent of whether AI could, in principle, perform equivalent analysis. Only a curricular redesign, not AI capability alone, could remove that dependency. Diffusion research further suggests institutional and pedagogical change of that kind tends to lag technical capability by a wide margin. The rating therefore holds at medium a decade out, anchored by course sequencing rather than by any judgment about AI's analytical ceiling.
MUS 1110.d: This course is the study of the melodic, harmonic, rhythmic, textural, and formal elements of music through analysis and composition, and the development of reading and hearing skills as they relate to these elements. It covers the elements of diatonic music commonly found in classical, jazz, and popular music styles, including Roman numeral and lead sheet analysis, and phrase structure and grouping. Aural and visual recognition of materials is emphasized.

r: This lab pairs with Music Theory I, applying reading and hearing skills to diatonic, triad-based music through singing, counting, and piano keyboard work. Unlike the theory lecture's written analysis, this is a live, performative skill: sight-singing intervals, counting rhythms aloud, and playing keyboard voicings in real time under instructor observation. That embodiment is directly protective, task-exposure research treats real-time, presence-dependent psychomotor work as comparatively low-exposure, and the verification burden is similarly high, since judging whether a student sang a pitch accurately or voiced a chord correctly on keyboard requires an attentive human ear in the room, not a document review after the fact. The course is also a required corequisite feeding directly into the continuing theory-lab sequence. Between the embodied, real-time nature of the work and its foundational role, this course rates low even before considering institutional designation, which is absent here.

By 2031, ear-training software may get better at drilling interval and rhythm recognition asynchronously, and some of that augmentation likely reaches this course as supplementary practice. But the core activity, singing pitches accurately, counting complex rhythms aloud, and performing keyboard voicings while an instructor listens and corrects in real time, remains resistant for the same reasons it is resistant today. The jagged-frontier finding that AI performance degrades sharply outside a system's competence zone is relevant: judging live vocal pitch accuracy and physical keyboard technique sits outside where digital assistants operate reliably. Embodiment and verification-burden dampeners both continue to apply, and the course's foundational role in the aural-skills sequence adds a further structural floor. The rating holds low at this horizon, with only modest uncertainty about hybrid drill-plus-instructor models emerging.

A decade out, hedging is warranted for exactly the same reason it is at nearer horizons: this course's tasks are physically embodied and real-time in a way that current capability-trend research, focused on digital and text-based task-time-horizons, does not directly address. Even substantial future gains in AI's general task competence may not translate into reliable live assessment of a student's singing pitch or keyboard technique, since that judgment depends on synchronous auditory and visual observation of a physical performance. The course's status as a required corequisite feeding the continuing theory-lab sequence adds a structural constraint independent of AI capability entirely. Diffusion patterns suggest that even capable technology often reaches embodied, relationship-dependent instruction last. The rating stays low at this horizon, reflecting durable protection from both the nature of the task and the course's place in the curriculum.
MUS 1120.d: Students apply reading and hearing skills to the melodic, harmonic, rhytlunic, textural, and formal elements of music through singing, counting, and the use of the piano keyboard. This course covers diatonic music based on the triad.

MUS 1130.d: This course is a continuation of MUS 1110. MUS 1140.d: This course is a continuation of MUS 1120, and covers diatonic material based on triads and seventh chords, and introduces chromaticism.

MUS 1210.d: Students explore the broad distinctions that define style and genre across a wide variety of musical traditions, including Western classical, jazz, global, and popular music. They become familiar with research methods and documentation techniques appropriate to music study, using both music databases and traditional library resources. Through this work, students build the foundational skills and knowledge necessary for success in more advanced music major courses.

r: MUS 1310 trains the singing actor in stage movement, facial and body gesture, and character research for opera performance, work tied directly to live vocal-physical coordination. Task-exposure research finds manual, physical, and real-time interpersonal work is the category least associated with AI exposure, and coaching this psychomotor skill requires an instructor's in-person judgment of breath support, gesture timing, and vocal health that generative tools cannot observe or correct live. Verification burden is high: a coach must catch technique that risks vocal injury, an error type AI cannot detect through observation alone. By 2031, AI-assisted rehearsal aids or generative research tools may supplement self-study of stage blocking or character backstory, marginally easing preparatory work outside the studio. But the graded core of MUS 1310, live coaching of gesture, breath, and vocal-physical integration under a faculty ear and eye, remains embodied, real-time, and psychomotor, the profile task-exposure research consistently ranks lowest for exposure. Diffusion data shows AI adoption remains uneven and gradual even where capable, and no acting-coaching product credibly replaces in-person direction of a singing actor's body. The instrumental need for this course is not measurably eroded at the five-year horizon; the rating stays Low with continued confidence.

Ten years out, capability trends point toward faster, more capable models, and rehearsal-support software may become genuinely useful for isolated tasks like character research or self-recorded movement review. Still, the defining work of MUS 1310 is real-time embodied coaching of a singer's physical instrument, a category task-exposure research places among the least automatable regardless of headline capability gains, since the constraint is presence and touch-level observation, not information processing. Any prediction this far out carries real uncertainty, and diffusion has historically lagged capability by years even in office settings, let alone live performance pedagogy. Absent a fundamental change in how embodied psychomotor coaching is delivered, the instrumental need for in-person acting-for-singers instruction should persist, though slow encroachment into adjacent prep tasks such as dramaturgical research is plausible. MUS 1310.d: This course offers a technical foundation in acting for the emerging opera singer. The singing actor is presented with unique challenges to expressive performance such as taking inspiration for the energy and tempo of stage movement from what one hears in the musical score, and learning to master facial and body gesture in a way which is powerfully communicative and at the same time not prohibitive to the process of healthy singing. In addition to acquiring tools to meet these challenges, students learn how to effectively research and develop operatic characters.

r: MUS 1650 teaches notation software, MIDI, signal flow, digital audio workstation operation, basic audio and video editing, copyright and licensing literacy, and music-website design, a fully digital skill set mapped to interacting with computers and processing information. Generative and assistive AI already handles adjacent tasks competently: automated mixing and mastering plugins, AI notation and transcription features, template-based website builders, and summarization of licensing terms. Verification burden is moderate; errors in licensing interpretation or signal routing are correctable rather than catastrophic. By 2031, AI-assisted DAWs, auto-mixing and mastering, generative notation, and no-code website builders are likely to be significantly more capable and more diffused, directly overlapping with this course's content: signal flow, editing workflows, licensing research, and site design. Productivity research on comparable digital tasks shows large speed gains from AI assistance, and the fully digital, non-embodied nature of this coursework places it among the more exposed profiles in task-exposure research. Verification burden remains only moderate since mistakes in licensing or audio processing are typically low-stakes and correctable. Diffusion data suggests firm-level adoption is still catching up to capability, tempering how fast instrumental need erodes, but the trajectory for this specific skill bundle points toward AI increasingly performing the mechanical portions of the work. Rating: High, moderate confidence given how quickly these consumer tools are evolving.

At ten years, capability-trend evidence showing rapid task-time-horizon doubling suggests AI tools for audio editing, notation, mixing, licensing lookup, and web design will likely be default-competent for most routine tasks this course teaches, though prediction this far out is necessarily uncertain. The course carries no general-studies designation and no accreditation-mandated credit floor tying a student to this specific class, and it is not a deep prerequisite gate for the broader curriculum, so no structural constraint protects it from substitution. Verification burden stays moderate rather than low, meaning AI-assisted output would still need some review, but not necessarily from someone trained in this exact course. Barring a shift in how foundational digital music-production literacy is taught, the instrumental need for this specific course is likely substantially diminished by 2036. Rating: High, moderate confidence.
MUS 1650.d: Students develop the technology skills necessary for contemporary musical practice. They learn to use music notation software, MIDI, microphones, and understand signal flow. Students gain experience with digital audio workstations, as well as basic digital audio and video editing and processing. They also explore topics in copyright, performing rights organizations, publishing, and music licensing, and design music-oriented websites.

MUS 1710.d: This course covers individual instruction in voice, piano, organ, guitar, electric bass, electric guitar, the standard band and orchestral instruments, composition, or conducting. It includes required weekly attendance at a one-hour performance class in the area of study in which students perform for one another. At the end of the semester, the student must successfully perform before a faculty jury committee in order to pass the course. This course may be repeated for credit in a different area of study.

r: MUS 2852 continues an applied sequence in which students study and perform the techniques, styles, and repertoire of artists within a chronological history of American popular music emphasizing rock 'n' roll. The course pairs embodied performance practice with historical-stylistic analysis. Task-exposure research places manual and real-time performance activity in the low-exposure category, and the performing component here is not a task AI executes on the student's behalf; a generative model can imitate a style, but it cannot substitute for a student developing the capacity to perform techniques and repertoire live. The historical-narrative portion is more exposed to AI-generated writing, yet that is a secondary strand layered on the applied-performance core. At 24 months, the instrumental need holds: the class's central deliverable is the student's own embodied musical competence, which automation augments but does not replace.

By 2031, AI music-generation and analysis tools will be considerably more capable, and the chronological-history and stylistic-analysis writing this course assigns becomes substantially easier to produce with AI assistance, consistent with observed-usage data showing writing tasks concentrated among the most AI-touched activities. The performance-practice strand, however, is real-time and psychomotor, and task-exposure research continues to treat that kind of embodied activity as low-exposure regardless of how fluent generative audio becomes. The instrumental case shifts: analytical and historical-summary work is increasingly AI-assisted, while the applied performing-and-imitating-technique work remains the course's protected core. Because both strands persist in the syllabus, the rating rises only to Medium rather than High — the written component erodes, but the embodied performance requirement keeps a real, un-automated task at the center of the course across a single catalog cycle.

A decade out, generative audio and AI music criticism should be pervasive and highly convincing under a central-case capability trajectory, given the pace implied by task-time-horizon doubling in current capability trend research. Even so, this course's performance strand — students physically performing an artist's techniques and repertoire — is not a task a model executes for the learner; embodiment keeps that portion instrumentally necessary. The historical-analytical strand is by then heavily automatable, and if the course leaned entirely on written history it would plausibly reach High. Because MUS 2852 combines applied performance with historical study, the rating holds at Medium. The central uncertainty concerns how the balance between performing and writing is taught and assessed as tools mature, not whether the embodied-performance component continues to anchor a real instrumental requirement.
MUS 2852.d: This course is the second course in a sequence. This course allows students to continue to study and perform the particular techniques, styles, repertoire, and sounds of artists within their proper historical, cultural, and social contexts. This course continues to outline a basic chronological history of American popular music with an emphasis on rock 'n' roll (broadly conceived).

r: MUS 2860 trains students to notate ideas as scores, lead sheets, and charts — conventional notation, drum charts, rhythm and slash notation, and the Nashville Number System — modeled on studio and touring industry practice. This is fundamentally a documentation and transcription skill, and observed-usage data show Computer & Mathematical and writing/office-style tasks as the heaviest categories of current AI use, a pattern audio-transcription and notation software increasingly extends into music. AI-assisted transcription tools already convert audio to notation and generate lead sheets with partial accuracy, offloading some of the course's mechanical transcription work even now. Full competence, though, still requires a human ear and judgment across multiple notation systems and genre conventions that current tools handle unevenly. At 24 months the course's instrumental need is already partially eroded on the mechanical side, which is why the rating starts at Medium rather than Low.

By 2031, automatic transcription and notation-generation tools should handle conventional Western notation, drum charts, and lead-sheet production with much greater reliability, consistent with the rapid task-time-horizon doubling documented in current capability trend research. The course's core deliverable — converting musical ideas into standard industry notation formats — is a well-specified, digitally native task of exactly the kind that automates fastest. Verification burden is moderate rather than high: a musician can check a generated chart against the audio relatively quickly, so errors are not especially costly or hard to catch. Embodiment is minimal since the work happens entirely in notation software. Under these conditions the instrumental need for a student to personally develop transcription and chart-writing skill erodes substantially, and the rating rises to High. Some hand-transcription competence likely persists as a check on AI output, tempering full certainty.

A decade out, under a central-case capability trajectory implied by continued rapid progress in AI systems, notation and chart-generation tools should be mature enough to convert recorded or described musical material into any of the formats this course teaches — Western notation, Nashville Number System, drum and rhythm charts — with high reliability. The task is digitally native, low-embodiment, and only moderately verification-sensitive, none of which protects it from automation at this horizon. The instrumental case for a student to personally master multi-system transcription is substantially weakened; what likely remains valuable is the aural judgment to catch AI transcription errors and adapt charts to unconventional material. The rating holds High, with the hedge that exactly how much residual hand-transcription skill programs continue to require, given quality-control needs, is genuinely uncertain this far out.
MUS 2860.d: In this course, students gain experience with the ability to communicate their ideas more effectively through written notation, using a variety of methods and techniques for producing scores, lead sheets, and charts. The course examines a range of pre-existing charts and scores from studio sessions and live tours for students to become more familiar with standard industry practices, and determining the ways that work best for their own compositions. Enhancing their musical literacy and aural skills, students transcribe songs from multiple genres, notating their various instrumental parts and vocals in a number of formats, including conventional Western notation, drum charts, rhythm and slash notation, and the Nashville Number System.

r: MUS 2862 teaches orchestration fundamentals for pop and rock ensembles: instrument ranges and functions for guitar, bass, drums, vocals, and piano, deconstructing existing rhythm sections and vocals, and building rearrangements, remixes, and original ensemble arrangements. Arranging is partly mechanical — voicing decisions, range-appropriate part-writing — and partly a creative judgment task about what a rearrangement should communicate. Task-exposure research associates programming- and writing-adjacent structured-composition work with higher exposure, and current AI arrangement and stem-separation tools already assist with deconstructing existing tracks and drafting rough arrangements. Full ensemble arranging that serves a specific creative and commercial purpose, however, still depends on a student's own developing judgment about instrumentation and idiom. At 24 months some mechanical arranging tasks are already assisted, but the course's core creative-arranging competence has not been meaningfully displaced, yielding Medium rather than Low.

By 2031, AI arrangement tools should draft idiomatic ensemble parts, remixes, and rearrangements with substantially more sophistication, aligning with the rapid capability growth documented in current AI trend research and with observed usage already concentrated in structured creative-technical tasks. The course's arranging work is fully digital, produced and revised in software, which limits any embodiment-based protection, and verification burden is moderate — a musician can judge whether an arrangement works without extensive specialized checking. Under these conditions the instrumental need for students to personally execute basic ensemble-arranging tasks erodes toward High. What plausibly persists is originality and stylistic intent behind a rearrangement, which AI drafts but does not independently conceive. The rating rises to High, tempered by real uncertainty about how quickly commercial arranging workflows actually adopt these tools versus using them as drafting aids.

Over a decade, under a central-case reading of continued rapid AI capability growth, arrangement-generation tools should competently produce genre-appropriate ensemble parts, rearrangements, and remixes across the instrumentation this course covers. The task remains digitally native and only moderately verification-sensitive, so little protects it from continued automation at this horizon. The instrumental case for personally executing standard arranging tasks is substantially eroded; the residual value lies in a musician's ability to direct, edit, and creatively redirect AI-drafted arrangements toward a specific artistic intent. The rating holds High. The genuine hedge is how arranging is taught and assessed a decade out — whether programs shift the course toward AI-assisted arranging direction rather than hand-arranging from scratch — a pedagogical question this rating does not resolve, though the instrumental need for hands-on arranging skill itself is diminished.
MUS 2862.d: This course focuses on transforming original raw song material into fully formed ensemble arrangements. Students are introduced to basic concepts in orchestration for the modern pop and rock ensemble: learning the fundamental attributes, functions, and ranges of the guitar, bass, drums, vocals, and piano in order to understand how to create viable arrangements for these instruments that work in multiple idioms. Students deconstruct the rhythm sections and vocals of existing songs to understand how and why they work as a unit. Students create re-arrangements and remixes of existing songs, but also work on ensemble arrangements of original material.

r: MUS 2864 extends the arranging sequence into more advanced orchestration: extended instrumental techniques, exploiting less obvious sonic possibilities on guitar, bass, drums, vocals, and piano, and incorporating strings, brass, woodwinds, mandolin, organ, and synthesizer into pop arrangements. This is a more nuanced creative-technical task than the introductory course, requiring judgment about unconventional instrument combinations and extended techniques that current AI arrangement tools handle unevenly. Task-exposure research still associates structured composition work with meaningful exposure, but the advanced, idiom-blending decisions this course targets sit closer to open-ended creative judgment than to templated part-writing. Current tools can suggest instrumentation but do not reliably produce sophisticated, idiomatically convincing arrangements across an expanded instrumental palette. At 24 months the instrumental need for a student to personally develop this advanced arranging judgment remains largely intact, supporting a Low rating.

By 2031, AI arrangement tools should be considerably better at incorporating strings, brass, and woodwinds and applying extended techniques, consistent with rapid capability growth documented in current AI trend research, but this advanced course's specific target — blending less-common instruments and techniques into convincing, idiomatic ensemble arrangements — remains a comparatively open-ended creative task even as more routine arranging automates. Verification burden is moderate: a musician can judge overall coherence without extensive specialized checking, which does not strongly protect the task, but the sophistication demanded here is a step beyond what the introductory arrangement course requires. The instrumental case erodes as tools mature but not as fully as in more mechanical notation or basic arranging work. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting partial but not complete erosion of the need to personally develop advanced orchestration judgment.

A decade out, under a central-case capability trajectory, AI arrangement systems should plausibly handle sophisticated multi-instrument orchestration, including strings, brass, woodwinds, and extended techniques, with much greater reliability than today. The task is digitally produced and only moderately verification-sensitive, so as capability catches up to this course's more advanced content, the protective gap relative to the introductory arranging course should narrow substantially. The instrumental need for a student to personally execute advanced orchestration tasks is then significantly eroded, though directing and evaluating AI-generated advanced arrangements for idiomatic and creative fit likely remains a human role. The rating rises to High, with real uncertainty about the pace of that catch-up — advanced, less-templated creative-technical tasks have historically lagged more routine automation, so this projection carries more hedge than the introductory arrangement course.
MUS 2864.d: Building on the first semester in this sequence (MUS 2862), this course continues to focus on transforming original raw song material into fully formed arrangements for contemporary ensembles. Students learn more advanced concepts in orchestration, including extended techniques and exploiting the sonic possibilities for guitar, bass, drums, vocals, and piano to create innovative arrangements of existing and original material. Students continue to deconstruct the rhythm sections and vocals of existing songs to understand how and why they work as a unit. Students explore the inclusion of strings, brass, and woodwinds into popular music, as well as other instruments common to pop arrangements, such as mandolin, organ, and synthesizer.

r: MUS 2865 refines lyric-writing craft: advanced techniques for subject matter and lyrics, critical deconstruction of existing lyrics across genres, and development of original lyrical content alongside reflection on the writer's own creative process. Lyric writing is squarely a writing task, and task-exposure research finds writing strongly positively associated with AI exposure; current large language models already generate fluent, genre-appropriate lyrics on demand. Verification burden here is comparatively low — a flawed AI-generated lyric produces mediocre art rather than a high-stakes error, so oversight is more about taste than expert correction, which is not strongly protective. The course's critical-deconstruction and reflective components add value AI generation does not supply to the learner, but the core generative task is already meaningfully automatable. That mix places the 24-month rating at Medium rather than Low.

By 2031, AI lyric generation should be reliably fluent and stylistically adaptable across the wide spectrum of genres this course studies, consistent with observed-usage data showing writing tasks concentrated among the heaviest current AI-use categories and with rapid capability growth documented in trend research. Verification burden remains low, since a mediocre AI lyric is a matter of artistic judgment rather than costly error, and the task is fully digital with no embodiment protection. The instrumental case for a student to personally generate lyrics from scratch weakens substantially, shifting more toward critically evaluating, editing, and directing AI-generated material and toward the reflective examination of one's own creative process, which the course also emphasizes. The rating rises to High. Some hedge remains around whether the course's critical and reflective components are enough to preserve a distinct pedagogical rationale.

A decade out, AI lyric generation should be highly capable and widely used across commercial songwriting under a central-case reading of continued rapid model progress. Lyric writing carries low verification burden and no embodiment protection, both factors that leave it exposed rather than shielded from automation at this horizon. The instrumental need for a student to personally draft original lyrics from a blank page is substantially diminished; what plausibly persists is the critical-deconstruction skill — reading and judging lyrics across genres — and reflective self-awareness of creative process, competencies the course already builds alongside generation. The rating holds High. The central uncertainty is not whether lyric generation automates, which seems likely, but whether critical judgment and creative-process reflection remain enough of an instrumental rationale to keep this course in place a decade out.
MUS 2865.d: Building on the previous course in this sequence, this course explores advanced techniques, methods, and practices for creating subject matter and lyrics. While refining previously learned methods, students are introduced to more advanced ways of conceptualizing lyric writing. Students critically examine and deconstruct a range of pre-existing lyrics from songwriters across a wide spectrum of genres and styles. Students refine their own artistic practices to create original lyrical content as well as reflect on their own creative process.

r: MUS 2866 has students write original songs for existing artists across multiple genres in response to specific prompts, applying notation skills from the prerequisite course, and explores how songwriters get noticed by industry acts. Writing to a brief for a target artist's style is a structured creative-writing task, and task-exposure research associates writing work with strong positive exposure; generative music tools already produce style-matched songs from prompts with growing commercial use. Verification burden is moderate — a poor style match is a professional miss rather than a high-stakes error — and the applied-notation component ties to a course already rated Medium at this horizon. Some of the course's prompt-response songwriting task is already assisted by current tools, but developing a personal command of matching brief, genre, and artist voice remains a live skill, keeping the 24-month rating at Medium.

By 2031, prompt-driven, style-matched song generation should be considerably more capable and more commercially normalized, consistent with observed-usage data on writing-task concentration and rapid capability growth documented in AI trend research; tools that generate songs matching a named artist's style from a brief are already an early version of exactly this course's target task. Verification burden stays moderate rather than protective, and the work is fully digital. The instrumental case for personally drafting song material to a commercial brief weakens substantially, shifting toward selecting, editing, and directing AI-generated material toward a specific artist's voice and toward the promotional and networking content the course also covers. The rating rises to High. A real hedge remains around how much of professional ghost-songwriting work actually migrates to AI-assisted workflows versus retaining human-led drafting by this horizon.

A decade out, under a central-case capability trajectory, style-matched song generation to a commercial brief should be a mature and widely deployed capability, given the pace of progress documented in current AI trend research. The task's digital nature and moderate verification burden do not meaningfully protect it at this horizon. The instrumental need for a student to personally draft songs for named artists from scratch is substantially eroded; more durable is judgment about artist voice, brief interpretation, and how to promote original work to industry acts, elements the course already addresses beyond pure drafting. The rating holds High. The genuine uncertainty is less about the drafting task's automatability, which appears likely, and more about how much of the commercial songwriting-for-hire market and its associated coursework persists in something like its current form.
MUS 2866.d: This course explores writing original material for existing established artists in numerous contemporary genres, including solo and group arrangements. Students develop a familiarity with the contemporary trends in multiple idioms to write for artists across a range of styles to specific prompts. Students also explore ways for young songwriters to promote and disseminate their own compositions to get noticed by industry-established acts. Students directly apply notation skills learned in Notation and Chart Writing.

r: MUS 2880 covers assessing and pursuing self-employment opportunities in music, starting and managing a music-related business, personal financial management for the self-employed, and navigating the industry's income volatility. This is applied small-business and personal-finance content — explaining business structures, budgeting practices, and financial planning — a domain where current AI systems already perform competently, similar to the general business-management content in comparable courses. Verification burden is moderate: financial and business guidance carries real consequences but this is educational rather than licensed financial advice, so errors are correctable rather than catastrophic. The material is entirely digital and knowledge-based, with no embodiment protection. AI already assists with drafting business plans and explaining self-employment finance basics, partially eroding the course's core content even now, which places the 24-month rating at Medium rather than Low.

By 2031, AI tools should handle routine small-business planning and personal-finance guidance for musicians with considerably more sophistication, in line with observed-usage data showing business and financial-planning tasks well represented in current AI use and rapid capability growth documented in trend research. The content is fully digital, and verification burden, while real, does not require the deep specialized expert-checking that would keep the rating protected — a self-employed musician can reasonably sanity-check AI-generated business guidance. The instrumental need for a student to learn this material primarily from a human instructor and personally work through the reasoning weakens substantially as AI becomes a competent on-demand advisor for exactly these questions. The rating rises to High. Some hedge remains: personal financial judgment under real volatility is harder to fully delegate than the informational content suggests.

A decade out, under a central-case capability trajectory, AI advisory tools should be a mature, widely adopted resource for small-business planning and personal financial management, a pattern consistent with continued rapid progress in AI systems. This course's content — business fundamentals and financial literacy for self-employed musicians — is digital, moderately verification-sensitive, and not protected by embodiment, all factors favoring continued erosion of the instrumental case for dedicated coursework. What plausibly remains valuable is applying that guidance to a musician's specific, volatile circumstances and exercising judgment under financial uncertainty in ways a general advisory tool does not fully replicate. The rating holds High. The primary uncertainty a decade out is less about the content's automatability, which seems substantial, and more about whether musicians actually adopt AI financial advising at scale.
MUS 2880.d: This course focuses on how to assess and exploit a variety self-employment opportunities available within the contemporary music industry. Students learn the fundamentals of starting and managing their own music-related business as well as how to manage their personal finances as they relate to self- employment. Recognizing the volatility of the music industry, students learn how to navigate times of abundance and scarcity.

r: MUS 2882 teaches how to break new artists into the mainstream music market through case-study analysis, exposure and reach-broadening strategies, marketing, networking, planning, problem-solving, and leadership. Much of this is relational and interpersonal — building industry relationships, leading a team around an artist, real-time negotiation and problem-solving — activities task-exposure research treats as comparatively low-exposure relative to pure writing or data-analysis work. The case-study and marketing-strategy analysis components are more exposed, since AI can synthesize case studies and draft marketing plans, but the course's networking and leadership emphasis keeps a meaningful embodied, real-time interpersonal core. Verification burden is moderate: a flawed strategy is a business setback rather than a catastrophic error. At 24 months the course's central competencies — networking, leadership, real-time strategic judgment — remain substantially un-automated, supporting a Low rating.

By 2031, AI should competently draft marketing strategies and synthesize case studies of how artists have broken into markets, consistent with observed-usage data on business-analysis tasks and rapid capability growth documented in AI trend research. That erodes the analytical-planning portion of the course. The networking and leadership components, however, involve real-time relationship-building and team leadership that task-exposure research continues to treat as lower-exposure interpersonal work, and no model performs those relational tasks on a student's behalf. The instrumental case splits: strategic-analysis work increasingly automates while the relational core persists. That mixed picture moves the rating to Medium rather than High. The hedge is substantial — how much of establishing-an-artist work becomes AI-assisted strategy paired with human relationship-building, versus something more fully automated, is genuinely unclear across a single catalog cycle.

A decade out, under a central-case capability trajectory, AI should handle strategic and marketing-analysis work for artist development with high reliability, and even relationship-oriented functions may be increasingly mediated by AI-assisted outreach and communication tools, narrowing the gap that protected the interpersonal core at earlier horizons. Verification burden stays moderate rather than strongly protective. The instrumental need for a student to personally develop case-study analysis, strategic planning, and even some networking-adjacent skills is substantially eroded under this trajectory. The rating rises to High. This carries real uncertainty, however: whether AI genuinely displaces human relationship-building and leadership in an industry built on personal trust and reputation, or whether those functions prove durably resistant even as analytical work automates, is not something this rating can confidently resolve at a ten-year horizon.
MUS 2882.d: Building on the artist and repertoire skills developed previously, in this course students focus on how to break (i.e., establish) new artists into the mainstream music industry. By examining a range of case studies, students learn to expose an artist to multiple audiences and broaden their reach to various markets. This class explores marketing strategies, networking, short and long term planning, problem solving, leadership, and other skills necessary to establish an artist in the contemporary music market.

r: MUS 2886 teaches artist income streams from an artist-manager's perspective: revenue diversification, long- and short-term financial planning, cost-benefit analysis, budget forecasting, cash-flow management, and communicating financial concepts to accountants, agents, banks, and investors. The quantitative core — forecasting, budgeting, cash-flow modeling — is structured financial-analysis work, a category well within current AI capability and consistent with observed-usage data showing Computer & Mathematical tasks as the largest current-usage category. Verification burden is moderate: forecasting errors have real consequences for an artist's finances, but this is educational content rather than licensed financial advice. The course's communication-with-stakeholders component adds an interpersonal element, but the dominant deliverables are quantitative models AI already assists with. At 24 months, the mechanical financial-analysis work is already meaningfully AI-assisted, which places this course's rating at Medium.

By 2031, AI financial-modeling and forecasting tools should handle budget forecasting, cash-flow management, and cost-benefit analysis for artist income streams with considerably greater sophistication, consistent with rapid capability growth documented in current AI trend research and with observed usage already concentrated in quantitative and Computer & Mathematical tasks. The material is fully digital, and verification burden, while real, is manageable without deep specialized expertise for most routine forecasting. The instrumental need for a student to personally build these financial models from first principles weakens substantially as AI becomes a competent forecasting assistant. What likely persists is the judgment to translate model output into advice for a specific artist and to communicate it credibly to accountants and investors. The rating rises to High, with some hedge around how quickly artist-management practice actually adopts AI financial tools.

A decade out, under a central-case capability trajectory, AI-driven financial forecasting and income-stream modeling for artists should be a mature, widely used capability, given the pace of progress documented in current AI trend research. The course's quantitative core is digital and only moderately verification-sensitive, offering little protection against continued automation at this horizon. The instrumental need for a student to personally execute financial modeling from scratch is substantially eroded; the more durable competency is translating financial outputs into concrete, defensible advice for an artist and communicating credibly with financial stakeholders. The rating holds High. The genuine uncertainty concerns how much artist-management education shifts toward interpreting and directing AI-generated financial analysis rather than building it by hand, not whether the underlying quantitative tasks themselves remain resistant to automation.
MUS 2886.d: This course focuses on understanding the various ways in which artists earn income from the perspective of an artist manager. This includes a survey of a multitude of income streams to create a diverse approach to creating, and advising on, revenue opportunities for artists. Students learn about long-term and short- term financial planning, cost-benefit analysis, budget forecasting, and cash flow management. Students develop a basic financial literacy as it relates to the music business, honing their ability to communicate with accountants, agents, banks, and third-party investors.

r: MUS 2888 examines how artist-development principles apply to non-US markets: stakeholder analysis, comparative legal structures, distribution channels, performance opportunities, marketing strategies, and historical and current international trends. This is comparative, research-heavy analytical work, which task-exposure research would generally treat as exposed, but the content spans multiple jurisdictions' legal and regulatory specifics — a domain where current AI systems are prone to confident, unverified errors, consistent with jagged-frontier findings that AI users score meaningfully less accurate outside a model's reliable range and exhibit miscalibrated trust. Getting cross-border legal and market claims wrong carries real consequences for an artist's international strategy, so verification burden is high rather than incidental. That verification demand, combined with the comparative-legal complexity, keeps genuine instrumental need for informed human analysis intact at 24 months, supporting a Low rating despite the topic's apparent research-task exposure.

By 2031, AI research and synthesis tools should be considerably better at comparative international market analysis, consistent with rapid capability growth documented in AI trend research, and the routine synthesis-and-summary portion of this course's work becomes easier to produce with AI assistance. But jurisdiction-specific legal and regulatory claims about non-US markets remain an area where hallucination risk and jagged-frontier miscalibration are a real concern for anyone using AI output for actual business decisions, keeping verification burden elevated. The instrumental case partially erodes — general market-trend synthesis is increasingly automatable — while the higher-stakes, cross-jurisdictional analytical judgment retains a real need for informed human checking. That split moves the rating to Medium rather than High. The hedge here is meaningful: how AI's cross-border legal reliability evolves over a single catalog cycle is genuinely uncertain.

A decade out, general AI research capability for comparative international market analysis should be substantially improved under a central-case capability trajectory, but jurisdiction-specific legal and regulatory accuracy across many national markets is a narrower, harder-to-verify domain than general synthesis, and jagged-frontier dynamics suggest confident errors in less-familiar regulatory territory remain a real risk even as overall capability rises. That sustained verification burden is the binding constraint keeping this course's rating from reaching High. The instrumental need for a student to develop genuine comparative-analytical judgment about international markets — not just AI-generated summaries of them — persists in the central case. The rating holds Medium. The considerable uncertainty is how reliably AI systems close the cross-jurisdictional accuracy gap over a decade, which this rating does not assume will be fully resolved.
MUS 2888.d: This course offers an overview of how principles learned in that class apply overseas. Students learn how to break and establish artists outside of the US market, including an introduction to, and analysis of, the primary stakeholders in the global music industry. This class explores the key similarities and differences between the US and non-US markets, including cultural dynamics, legal structures, distribution channels, performance opportunities, and marketing strategies. Students also examine historical and current trends in various overseas markets and discuss how artists stay relevant over time.

r: Home Recording teaches multi-track recording technique, mixing, and mastering so students can produce home recordings to a professional standard, capturing instruments and ensembles across varied hardware and software — work mapped to sound-engineering activities like interacting with computers, documenting information, and analyzing audio signals. Automated mixing and mastering services already perform loudness balancing, EQ correction, and noise reduction competently, and observed-usage data identifies Computer & Mathematical work as the largest AI-usage category, with productivity research showing large task-speed gains from AI-assisted technical workflows. The course carries no general-studies designation and no accreditation lock, so no institutional brake protects it. At 24 months students still need hands-on signal-chain and monitoring judgment that automated services do not fully replace, but the instrumental rationale for teaching every mixing step by hand is already eroding as these tools diffuse into home-studio practice.

By 2031, AI-assisted mixing and mastering tools will handle a substantially larger share of the production chain, including arrangement-aware balancing and mastering tuned to genre and platform, and diffusion data on rising firm-level AI adoption suggests these consumer-grade tools will be common in home-studio workflows well before then. Task-exposure research classifies technical production and editing work as positively associated with automation exposure. With no general-studies designation, accreditation mandate, or embodiment protecting it, and only moderate verification burden around aesthetic judgment, the course's instrumental case for manually executing every recording and mixing step weakens substantially. The rating rises to High: producing a professional-standard home recording increasingly means directing and correcting AI tools rather than performing each mixing and mastering operation by hand, though genuinely novel material and equipment choices still require human judgment.

A decade out, AI-assisted production tools plausibly handle the great majority of routine multi-track recording, mixing, and mastering work to a professional standard, following the capability trend of rapidly lengthening task-time horizons for AI systems. The course's applied tasks are digital, non-adversarial, and low in error cost, so verification burden does not meaningfully protect them, and no institutional or foundational constraint caps the rating at this horizon either. The instrumental case for learning manual mixing-console and mastering-chain execution is substantially eroded in the central case. The rating holds High, hedged by genuine uncertainty about how much creative and technical judgment in capturing performances and shaping a mix remains resistant to automation, and by how quickly diffusion into home-studio and educational contexts actually proceeds.
MUS 2890.d: This course covers the fundamentals of multi-track recording techniques, mixing, and mastering, enabling students to produce their own home recordings to a professional standard. Students learn to record a range of instruments and ensembles using numerous types of hardware and software.

r: Techniques and Improvisation I builds technical facility on the student's chosen instrument and improvisational fluency across musical contexts through a progression of intermediate exercises and applied practice — real-time psychomotor and interpretive skill development that maps to performing-for-an-audience and creative-thinking activities rather than any task an AI model executes on a student's behalf. Generative audio models can produce improvised-sounding music, but they do not substitute for a student developing the physical instrumental technique and in-the-moment musical judgment the course cultivates. Task-exposure research places manual and psychomotor skill acquisition well outside AI's automatable range even as programming and writing exposure rises elsewhere. At 24 months there is no meaningful erosion: the instrumental need is the embodied, real-time competence itself, which the course exists specifically to develop through supervised practice.

By 2031, AI music-generation tools will be considerably more capable and may reshape parts of the commercial and educational music landscape, including practice aids and generative accompaniment. That is a tooling and market question, distinct from whether a student must still develop the physical technique and improvisational instinct this course builds. The applied competence remains embodied and real-time, and verification of a student's playing still requires a knowledgeable instructor listening in person, keeping the human necessary to the pedagogical act itself. Across one catalog cycle the applied-instruction requirement is unlikely to be restructured away. The rating remains Low: AI may increasingly assist practice and accompaniment, but it does not perform the instrumental-technique development the course is built to deliver, and the embodied nature of the skill resists substitution even as surrounding tools improve.

Under a wide-uncertainty central case, AI-generated and AI-assisted music tools will be pervasive and highly capable by 2036, and practice technology may look very different from today's. Even so, the specific competence Techniques and Improvisation I develops — a musician's own physical facility and improvisational judgment, exercised live — is not a task that AI performs for the student; the entire point is embodied skill formation through repetition and feedback. The most plausible decade-scale change concerns how AI tools enter practice and pedagogy, not whether learning to play and improvise still requires doing it oneself. The rating holds Low, with the caveat that the broader labor market for improvising musicians is far more exposed to generative-audio competition than the instrumental necessity of this applied-instruction course.
MUS 2910.d: Building upon Techniques and Improv I and II, this course provides students the opportunity to further develop technical facility on their chosen instrument along with a deeper understanding of improvisatory skills. This involves a logical progression of intermediate level exercises and application. Students are challenged to experiment with intermediate level techniques to further develop a creative approach to improvisation. The course situates intermediate technical vocabulary and improvisational skills within a variety of musical contexts across numerous genres.

r: Building directly on Techniques and Improvisation I, this course advances technical facility and improvisational ability through advanced-intermediate exercises applied across challenging and varied musical contexts — continued embodied, real-time skill development rather than any task performable by an AI system on the student's behalf. The relevant work activities are psychomotor instrument technique and live creative musical judgment, categories task-exposure research does not treat as meaningfully automatable even as it finds programming and writing strongly exposed. Generative audio tools can produce plausible improvisations, but they do not build a student's own facility or spontaneous musical reasoning. At 24 months the instrumental need is intact and undiminished: the course's entire content is the supervised cultivation of a physical and interpretive skill that only practice develops.

By 2031, generative-audio systems will likely be integrated into practice software and production pipelines, and the surrounding commercial landscape for improvising musicians may shift as AI tools mature — a market question that sits outside this rating. The question of instrumental necessity is unchanged: an advanced-intermediate improviser still has to build technique and instinct through live playing, and an instructor's in-person evaluation of tone, timing, and interpretive choices remains the practical way to verify progress, keeping human expertise necessary to the pedagogical process. The most plausible ten-year shift concerns how AI enters rehearsal, feedback, and accompaniment, not whether learning to play and improvise at an advancing level still requires doing so oneself. The rating holds Low, with the honest caveat that the commercial context surrounding improvising musicians is considerably more exposed than the instrumental necessity of this applied-instruction course.
MUS 2920.d: This course builds directly on MUS 2910: Intermediate Techniques and Improv I, providing students an opportunity to further develop technical facility on their chosen instrument while advancing their improvisational abilities. This involves a logical progression of advanced-intermediate exercises and applications. Students experiment with an advanced-intermediate level of techniques to further develop a creative approach to improvisation. The class situates technical vocabulary and improvisational skills within a variety of challenging musical contexts across numerous genres at an advanced-intermediate level.

The rating remains Low: AI tools may support practice between sessions, but they do not perform the embodied instruction this course exists to deliver.

The most plausible ten-year change is in how much AI-assisted practice tools supplement classroom instruction, not in whether beginning students still need supervised, embodied group instruction to acquire the skill at all. MUS 2940.d: This class offers group instruction on an instrument to students with little or no previous training.

r: Musics of America surveys the African, Indigenous, Hispanic, Asian, and European colonial threads of American music, developing students' understanding of style, aesthetics, and function across folk, religious, classical, popular, and commercial traditions within their sociocultural context — work mapped to getting and interpreting information and communicating analysis to others, a listening-and-writing course rather than performance. Written analysis is exposed to AI, but the course carries a General Studies: Arts and Humanities designation, a GT-Pathways-type mandate that locks its place in the transfer core regardless of task automatability. By 2031, AI will fluently generate stylistic and sociocultural analysis of American musical traditions, weakening the rationale for students to produce that writing unaided. Task-exposure research classifies this kind of analytical writing among positively-exposed activities, and observed-usage data shows writing and office-style tasks are already prominent in AI use. The instrumental case shifts toward the student's own cultivated listening skill and toward evaluating AI-generated analysis for accuracy and nuance, especially given the sociocultural sensitivity of the material. The Arts and Humanities general-studies designation caps the erosion at Medium by holding the course in the transfer core across a catalog cycle. The rating rises to Medium: the written-analysis artifacts increasingly automate, but the general-education mandate and the listening literacy the course builds keep it instrumentally necessary.

A decade out, AI produces sophisticated musical and sociocultural analysis on demand, and the case for students composing that analysis unaided is substantially eroded, consistent with capability-trend projections of rapidly lengthening AI task-time horizons. But the general-education Arts and Humanities requirement persists in the central case, and the cultivated capacity to listen critically across African American, Indigenous, and immigrant musical traditions retains instrumental value the AI-generated artifact does not supply the learner directly. The rating holds Medium, capped by the transfer mandate from either rising to High or, absent the mandate, falling to Low. The genuine uncertainty is how appreciation-and-analysis courses are taught and assessed once AI writes fluent commentary by default, not whether the general-education requirement and the listening-literacy goal it protects remain in force.
MUS 3000.d: This course explores American music and its unique blend of African, Indigenous, Hispanic, Asian, and European colonial musical styles and genres. Students develop an understanding of the musical style, aesthetic viewpoints, and function of the folk, religious, classical, popular, and commercial musics of these groups. The course materials also consider the interaction of these musical styles and genres within the context of sociocultural dynamics of the United States. The students encounter a broad variety of musical expressions and study those expressions within the context of culture.

Task-exposure research finds critical and interpretive writing positively associated with automation exposure, and productivity research on professional writing shows AI cutting composition time substantially while raising output quality. The instrumental case shifts toward evaluating AI-generated cultural analysis for bias, nuance, and accuracy on genuinely contested topics like cultural hegemony and transnational identity. The dual Arts and Humanities and Global Diversity designation caps the erosion at Medium by preserving the course's place in the general-education core across a catalog cycle. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting substantial but not unbounded erosion of the writing-execution rationale at this horizon.

The rating holds Medium, capped by the transfer mandate against rising to High. The open question is how discussion-based courses on contested cultural material are taught and assessed once AI drafts sophisticated commentary by default, not whether the general-education requirement protecting the course's place in the curriculum remains in force.
MUS 3015.d: Students explore musical thought and processes through an examination of the development of "world music" and "world beat" in the 20th and 21st century, including its meaning and importance to contemporary culture as well as its history and impact. Students address the complex relationships of music and mass media while addressing themes of nationalism, popular resistance and subversion, censorship, transnational identity, gender representation, and cultural hegemony in popular music.

r: History of Jazz surveys American jazz as African American musical expression, from minstrelsy and ragtime through blues, bebop, and current trends, developing active-listening skills alongside historical understanding through listening, reading, and performing — work mapped to getting historical information and interpreting musical and cultural meaning for others. By 2031, AI will fluently narrate jazz history and generate stylistic commentary on musical eras and figures, weakening the rationale for students producing that narrative writing themselves. Task-exposure research classifies historical narrative and synthesis as positively exposed, while the course's active-listening component — discerning musical elements by ear across eras and styles — is comparatively resistant, since it builds a perceptual skill rather than a textual artifact alone. The instrumental case shifts toward listening literacy and toward evaluating whether AI-generated jazz history accurately centers African American musicians' agency rather than flattening it. The Arts and Humanities designation caps the erosion at Medium by preserving the course's transfer-core status across a catalog cycle. The rating rises to Medium accordingly, reflecting eroded writing execution but a protected curricular place.

A decade out, AI produces detailed, well-organized jazz-history narratives on demand, and the rationale for students composing that narrative unaided is substantially eroded, consistent with capability-trend projections of longer AI task horizons. The general-education Arts and Humanities requirement persists in the central case, though, and the cultivated capacity for active, discerning listening — distinguishing style, technique, and historical lineage by ear — retains instrumental value the AI-generated text does not supply directly to the learner. The rating holds Medium, capped by the transfer mandate against reaching High. The genuine uncertainty concerns how a course centered on African American musical experience and critical listening is taught and assessed once AI writes fluent jazz history by default, not whether the general-education requirement anchoring the course persists.
MUS 3020.d: In this class, students explore the many facets of American jazz as a history of African American musical expression. Through a survey of important events and major figures, including their effect on music through their actions and those of their followers, students learn the tools of active listening by gaining a greater understanding of the musical elements through listening, reading, and performing. The course covers minstrelsy, ragtime, blues, New Orleans and classic jazz, bebop and related movements, as well as current trends of the genre. This course centralizes the perspective that jazz is inexorably tied to the experience of African American musicians, who simultaneously were influenced by and responded to the dominant culture of popular music in the creation of something new.

MUS 3030.d: This course examines the music and musicians that contribute to the development of improvisation in American folk music outside of the tradition of Jazz. This course surveys the phenomenon of "Americana," music which is derived from the various forms of American roots music, comprised of the wide variety of cultural practices found in the United States. The blues, bluegrass, Appalachian music, and other culturally varied forms of American improvised music are covered.
