MUS 3050.d: This course explores the diverse forms of musical expression found within cultures from around the world. In addition to surveying a variety of musical practices, aesthetic systems, and functions of music, the fundamental theoretical approaches of ethnomusicology are introduced and employed. Through an exploration of case studies selected from diverse music cultures, the course focuses on topics such as identity, race, ethnicity, gender, class, religion, memory, migration, globalization, tourism, social, and political movements.

r: This course asks students to trace blues technique across genres, analyze how Bessie Smith, Robert Johnson, and B.B. King's recordings encode African American historical experience, and write critically about the commercial appropriation of Black musical labor. A general-purpose model can already draft a passable chronological survey linking blues to gospel, jazz, and hip hop, since that narrative is well documented online, but the course's core work of connecting sonic technique to lived marginalization sits closer to the critical-interpretive domain that task-exposure research finds negatively associated with model exposure. Verification burden stays meaningful: AI drafts on race and appropriation risk flattening nuance an instructor must catch. The course also carries a General Studies Arts and Humanities designation, a gtPathways-style transfer mandate that keeps enrollment demand structurally protected at this horizon.

By 2031, generative tools will likely draft fluent thematic essays linking blues idioms to soul, funk, and hip hop, and observed-usage data already shows writing tasks concentrated among the most AI-touched activities, so students' rough-draft synthesis work becomes considerably more automatable. What stays harder to offload is the seminar's central purpose: guided critical engagement with how Black cultural expression was commodified and whose voices get centered, which depends on an instructor's disciplinary judgment to evaluate nuance and correct culturally insensitive output. That verification burden keeps the course's instrumental value from collapsing even as drafting assistance spreads. The General Studies Arts and Humanities designation continues guaranteeing institutional demand independent of automation trends, since gen-ed transfer requirements are set by state policy rather than by how well a model writes about Bessie Smith.

A decade out, capability trends such as the roughly four-to-seven-month doubling of AI task-time horizons documented by METR and Epoch suggest models will handle historical synthesis and structured argument drafting for a course like this quite fluently, pushing realized automatability toward the upper range if adoption keeps pace. Even so, this is a hedge, not a prediction: firm-level adoption remains well under half of US businesses per Census BTOS diffusion data, and a seminar built around live discussion of appropriation and cultural ownership retains a verification and facilitation core that a professor's disciplinary judgment underwrites. The General Studies designation is a structural floor unrelated to AI capability, keeping the course inside the transfer core. Expect meaningful erosion of rote survey-writing value rather than elimination of the course's institutional function.
MUS 3051.d: Students in this class explore African American musical heritage, from the Transatlantic slave trade through to music and the Black Lives Matter movement. We engage with the blues not only as a genre but also as a set of techniques and approaches that have shaped American music and culture. From the 19th century to today, we look at how the blues has influenced genres such as jazz, gospel, rock, soul, funk, country, and hip hop. Through a study of iconic figures like Bessie Smith, Robert Johnson, and B.B. King, we examine the mainstream blues tradition, while also uncovering its deeper roots and impact on various other musical styles. As we trace the evolution of the music, students gain insight into how the blues has served as a metaphor for African American experiences and cultural expression, and how it has shaped American identity as a whole. Additionally, we explore the ways in which Black cultural expressions, including the blues, have been co-opted for mainstream profit, while the musicians who created them often faced marginalization, exploitation, and erasure. Course content encourages you to think critically about the intersection of music, history, and culture, and how African American musical legacies continue to resonate in today's world.

r: This methods course prepares elementary generalists to teach art and music, integrating literacy and math, through hands-on studio practice alongside philosophical and aesthetic content. Lesson-plan drafting and integration-strategy templates are increasingly generated with AI assistance, a use case where productivity research shows the largest uplift for novice practitioners, which describes most students here. But judging whether an integrated art-music lesson is developmentally appropriate for elementary learners, and building the studio craft and artistic sensibility the description names, both require an instructor's direct modeling and in-person feedback that current tools cannot substitute for. That embodied, judgment-heavy core keeps realized automatability low at this horizon despite AI's growing usefulness for administrative lesson-plan scaffolding. No general studies designation constrains the course, so any future erosion tracks capability rather than institutional lock-in.

By 2031, AI-assisted lesson planning and curriculum-integration drafting should be routine, and the jagged-frontier research on human-AI collaboration suggests students will lean on these tools confidently for the parts of the course that resemble document generation, while remaining at risk of overconfidence on the pedagogical judgment calls that fall outside a model's reliable range. The instrumental case for the drafting and planning components accordingly weakens. What remains protected is guided studio practice in developing artistic sensibility and critical judgment about what makes an integrated lesson pedagogically sound, work that still depends on an instructor's direct feedback loop with a novice teacher-in-training. With no general studies designation and no licensure-clinical mandate specific to this course, the rating moves to Medium as the planning-adjacent tasks become substantially automatable while the applied teaching-craft core resists.

Ten years out, if AI capability keeps advancing at anything like the pace METR and Epoch document, tools should competently generate differentiated, standards-aligned art-and-music lesson sequences and even model classroom scenarios for practice, narrowing the course's unique instrumental contribution substantially. This is a hedge rather than a confident forecast, since Census BTOS diffusion data shows adoption still uneven across institutions today and elementary teacher-prep practice tends to be slow to change even where the underlying technology is ready. Absent a general studies or licensure-clinical designation capping the course, and with no critical-prerequisite role for later required courses, little structurally protects it from this drift. The rating rises to High, reflecting genuine uncertainty about how quickly methods instruction itself gets redesigned around AI-assisted planning tools rather than certainty that it will.
MUS 3060.d: This course enables students to develop awareness and knowledge of philosophical and aesthetic foundations of the arts with a specific focus on art and music. Appropriate methods of teaching art and music in the elementary curriculum, including the integration of literacy and mathematics, will be explored. Students will use creative and critical thinking skills to develop artistic sensibility.

r: Students here compose original lyrics, melody, and harmony and document songs for performance across genres, exactly the kind of generative creative-writing task that consumer AI music and lyric tools already perform at a rough-draft level, consistent with task-exposure research finding writing strongly positively associated with model exposure. This projection carries real uncertainty, since diffusion data shows adoption lagging capability broadly and songwriting pedagogy may adapt around AI-assisted composition rather than being displaced by it. Absent any general studies designation, licensure mandate, or foundational role protecting the course, the rating rises to High, acknowledging that the instrumental case for manually developing these compositional mechanics is the most exposed among this batch's craft courses.
MUS 3070.d: This course provides students with the introduction of the basic aesthetic and communicative concepts of songwriting with regard to tradition and to contemporary trends, enabling students to articulate a conscious method appropriate to their own aesthetic approaches to songwriting. Students compose original songs with various features (lyrics, melody, harmony, etc.) and document them for communication and performance in various genres, styles, and situations.

r: Counterpoint teaches species writing, fugal technique, and stylistic composition in the idioms of Palestrina, Bach, Shostakovich, and Hindemith, work governed by codified voice-leading rules that make it unusually rule-based for a humanities subject, closer to the pattern-completion tasks task-exposure research associates with programming and formal-systems exposure. AI tools already generate reasonably competent species counterpoint and can flag rule violations like parallel fifths, since the constraints are explicit and well-represented in training data. Verification burden is moderate rather than low: judging whether a passage genuinely captures Bach's or Shostakovich's idiom, not just rule compliance, still needs a trained ear. By 2031, AI composition tools should handle rule-governed contrapuntal writing across all three studied eras fluently, and GDPval-style benchmarks already show top models approaching parity with expert output on structured technical deliverables, a category this course's species-writing and fugue exercises resemble closely and consistently across assignments and eras studied. With verification burden only moderate, since stylistic fidelity checks, while requiring expertise, are more tractable than open-ended critical judgment, and with no general studies designation, licensure mandate, or critical-prerequisite role capping the rating, the instrumental case for students to master these techniques by hand erodes substantially over this window of time. The rating rises to High, reflecting a rule-based skill domain where formal-systems capability growth translates relatively directly into realized task automation.

Ten years out, under continued METR/Epoch-style capability growth in structured technical domains, AI should reliably generate stylistically convincing counterpoint across historical idioms with minimal expert correction, which would leave little of this course's applied composition-and-analysis work instrumentally necessary by the standards this rating applies to comparable coursework across the curriculum. This projection is hedged: adoption of AI composition tools inside conservatory-style theory sequences may lag capability for pedagogical or accreditation-culture reasons even where technically feasible, and instructors may deliberately preserve hand-composition exercises for skill-building independent of whether an automated alternative exists in the market. But nothing in the course's institutional profile, no general studies designation, no licensure mandate, no critical-prerequisite chain of any kind, caps the rating, so it remains firmly High.
MUS 3100.d: This course introduces students to the contrapuntal styles of the 16th, 18th, and 20th centuries. Topics include species counterpoint of the 16th century, the fugal process of the 18th century, and the contrapuntal techniques and devices of the 20th century. Representative composers include Palestrina and Gesualdo (16th), J. S. Bach (18th), and Shostakovich and Hindemith (20th). The course includes both analysis of and composition in the styles of each of the three eras.

r: This course covers arranging and orchestration technique, notation for individual instruments and ensembles, chord voicing and substitution, microphone technique for live and studio recording, and the business layer of copyright, licensing, and Performing Rights Organizations. That mix of notation-based composition work and hands-on audio-engineering and legal-practice content keeps realized automatability moderate rather than high right now: AI notation assistants can suggest voicings and orchestration choices, but judging professional-grade orchestral balance and giving reliable licensing guidance both carry real error cost if wrong, consistent with the elevated verification burden the jagged frontier research documents when AI users operate outside a tool's reliable range. No general studies designation or foundational-prerequisite role constrains the course structurally, so the Low rating here reflects task characteristics, particularly verification burden, rather than institutional lock-in.

By 2031, AI orchestration and arranging assistants should handle a larger share of the notation and voicing work competently, and observed usage data already shows writing- and drafting-adjacent tasks concentrated among heavily AI-touched activities, consistent with faster uptake for the compositional side of this course than for its audio-engineering and legal content specifically. Verification burden eases somewhat as tools improve at flagging orchestrational and copyright-compliance issues, though professional-quality judgment about balance and licensing risk still benefits from expert review at this horizon and probably beyond it. With no general studies designation or prerequisite chain to other courses in this cluster, the rating moves to Medium, tracking capability growth on the notation-heavy portion of the syllabus rather than the microphone-technique and licensing portions.

A decade out, if AI arranging tools continue to improve at anything like the pace METR and Epoch document for task-time horizons, competent full orchestral arrangements, harmonic reharmonizations, and even preliminary licensing guidance should be achievable with limited expert correction, substantially eroding the instrumental case for learning this content by hand from first principles across most of the syllabus and its professional-standards material. Genuine uncertainty remains about how much of the professional publishing and studio-microphone-technique content resists automation because it depends on situational audio judgment rather than notation rules that a model can pattern-match against training data alone. Absent any general studies designation, licensure mandate, or critical-prerequisite function of any kind, nothing structurally caps the course, so the rating rises to High.
MUS 3150.d: The study of the technical capabilities and notation of all the instruments and voices, individually and in ensembles. Presentation of historical and contemporary arranging and orchestration techniques, including professional standards for publishing and for recording. Presentation of professional expectations and courtesies. Presentation of appropriate harmonic structures for various genres including appropriate chord voicing and chord substitution (including negative harmonies). Microphone techniques for all instruments/voices for both the concert (live) and studio environments. Since arrangements and orchestrations must be licensed in the professional environment, copyright infringement, Performing Rights Organizations, and music licensing procedures are also discussed. In addition to standard professional ensembles, multiple academic ensembles and world music ensembles are also covered during course of the semester.

r: This one-credit course has students study idiomatic combo and big-band arranging techniques from Ellington, Basie, Mingus, and peers, then write and hear their own arrangement performed live in class by classmates on real instruments. That live-performance feedback loop is the pedagogical center: the student writes for real instrumentalists, hears the result, and adjusts in real time, an embodied, interpersonal process task-exposure research does not classify as automatable in any meaningful sense. Judging whether a jazz arrangement captures authentic swing feel, idiomatic voicing, and big-band balance is a subtle, culturally specific aesthetic judgment that keeps verification burden high, meaning AI output cannot be trusted without an expert jazz musician's ear checking it. Both factors bind hard at this horizon, holding the rating at Low regardless of general studies status or how capable text-based AI arranging assistance becomes.

By 2031, AI arranging assistants will likely generate passable big-band voicings on request, and some students may use such tools to accelerate first-draft sketching before class. But the course's actual instrumental output, an arrangement performed live in class for immediate aural feedback from a jazz combo or big band, keeps the embodied, real-time performance loop central and non-substitutable no matter how the drafting stage evolves. The jagged-frontier research on human-AI collaboration is a caution here: relying on AI arranging output without a trained jazz ear to catch idiomatic missteps risks confidently wrong results reaching the bandstand. Verification burden and embodiment both stay low, protective in this framework's terms, so the rating holds at Low even as adoption of AI drafting assistance elsewhere in music technology grows steadily.

A decade out, this course's rating remains the most protected in the batch because its defining task, composing for and hearing a live big-band or combo performance, structurally requires embodied, in-person musicianship that no plausible near-term AI capability substitutes for on the student's behalf. Even under aggressive capability-growth assumptions like those METR and Epoch document for other, more digitally native domains, the verification and embodiment constraints here are intrinsic to the pedagogy itself rather than a function of AI's raw generative ability at producing notated arrangements. Some hedge is warranted: AI drafting tools may reduce time spent on rote notation work well before 2036, shifting how students sketch first drafts. But the rating holds at Low, tracking the MUS 2730-style applied and ensemble courses anchoring this framework.
MUS 3160.d: This course gives students the skills needed to arrange for jazz combo and big band. Techniques studied include those employed by composer/arrangers such as Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Miles Davis, Fletcher Henderson, Duke Ellington, Count Basie, Billy Strayhorn, Bill Evans, Charles Mingus, Sun Ra, Toshiko Akiyoshi, Thad Jones, and Maria Schneider. The students create their own arrangement for jazz combo and big band that is played in class.

r: This course trains prospective music educators to arrange functional performance material for whatever instrumentation their future school ensemble happens to have, plus rudimentary orchestration skills, a practical, constraint-driven notation task well suited to AI assistance since the request pattern, arrange this piece for these specific instruments, is exactly the kind of scoped drafting task current tools already handle reasonably well. Verification burden is moderate: a teacher can usually tell quickly whether a generated arrangement is playable by their available students, lowering the error cost relative to professional publishing contexts where a wrong voicing carries real reputational or financial stakes. No general studies designation or critical-prerequisite role constrains the course structurally. The rating starts at Medium, reflecting real but incomplete realized automatability of this scoped, rule-based arranging task at this horizon.

By 2031, AI arranging tools should handle constrained-instrumentation arranging requests fluently, and productivity research on AI assistance shows the largest gains accruing to less experienced practitioners, a good description of undergraduate music-education students learning this skill for the first time in their training. Because the task is narrowly scoped and self-verifiable by a classroom teacher checking playability against their own roster, the moderate verification burden that holds the rating down at 24 months eases further as tools mature and gain wider classroom adoption. With no institutional designation or foundational role protecting the course, the rating rises to High: the specific instrumental skill of manually voicing arrangements for ad hoc ensembles is substantially superseded by tools that do this competently on request.

A decade out, if AI capability keeps growing at the pace METR and Epoch document, generating a playable arrangement for an arbitrary, non-standard school-ensemble instrumentation should be a solved, low-effort request, which would leave little instrumental rationale for a dedicated course teaching students to do this by hand from first principles. Some hedge is warranted: teacher-preparation programs may retain hands-on arranging instruction for pedagogical reasons, to build teachers' own musical literacy and classroom improvisational fluency in front of real students on short notice, independent of whether AI can produce the artifact, and Census BTOS diffusion data suggests adoption inside teacher-prep curricula could lag general capability trends. Absent any general studies or licensure-clinical designation on this specific course, though, the rating stays High.
MUS 3170.d: This course provides the prospective music educator with the skills needed to create functional performance material for the instrumentation at their disposal, as well as introducing rudimentary orchestration and arranging skills.

r: This variable-topics seminar studies the history and literature of a single style, era, medium, or composer chosen by the instructor, meaning the specific research and writing tasks shift every offering. Because the topic can be narrow or under-documented (a specific regional tradition or lesser-known composer, for instance), verification burden stays elevated at this horizon: the jagged-frontier research on human-AI collaboration warns that AI users score worse outside a model's reliable range, and specialized musicological topics are exactly where a model is more likely to fabricate sources or misattribute scholarship. That variability, combined with no general studies designation, keeps the realized-automatability rating at Low for now despite AI's general strength at historical writing tasks. Confidence in this rating is lower than for fixed-topic courses given the description's variable scope.

By 2031, AI research and writing assistance for musicological topics should improve substantially, and observed-usage data already shows writing and research-synthesis tasks concentrated among the most AI-touched activities, suggesting students will increasingly draft topic essays and literature reviews with heavy AI involvement regardless of how niche the semester's chosen topic happens to be. Verification burden likely eases as retrieval-augmented tools reduce fabrication risk on less-documented topics, though it does not disappear given the deliberately variable, sometimes obscure subject matter the instructor may choose each term for each offering. With no general studies designation or prerequisite role protecting the course, the rating moves to Medium, tracking general capability growth in historical-research writing while acknowledging the topic-dependent uncertainty this variable-content course carries.

A decade out, if AI research capability keeps advancing per METR and Epoch's documented trend and GDPval-style benchmarks showing models approaching expert parity on realistic research deliverables, this course's core work, producing a well-sourced study of a chosen musical topic, should be substantially reproducible by AI with limited human correction even for less mainstream subjects than the mainstream repertoire covered elsewhere in the catalog. This is hedged: instructor-chosen topics could deliberately target underdocumented repertoire specifically because it resists easy AI synthesis, which would keep realized automatability lower than the general trend implies for any given offering of this variable-topics course. Absent any general studies designation or foundational role, though, nothing structurally caps the course, and the rating rises to High.
MUS 3200.d: This course is designed to study the history and literature of a single musical style, era, medium, or composer.

r: This required survey traces Western music from Ancient Greek theory through medieval polyphony, Renaissance style, and the Baroque era via score and recording analysis, well-documented, digitized content that AI already summarizes and analyzes competently, since consensus historical facts about early music carry lower verification burden than contested cultural interpretation. The course sits fully in the digital domain: no ensemble or applied-performance component, just analysis of recordings and scores. What holds the rating to Medium rather than higher at this horizon is its foundational scaffolding role, it is the entry point in a music-history sequence that upper-level courses like variable-topics seminars build on, requiring the sequence's continuity even as individual analytical tasks become automatable. No general studies designation applies; the constraint here is curricular sequencing, not gen-ed transfer.

By 2031, AI tools should handle score and recording analysis across this survey's full historical range fluently, and GDPval-style benchmarks already show top models approaching expert parity on structured research deliverables resembling this course's written analytical work closely and consistently across topics. Verification burden continues easing for early-music history specifically, since this period's scholarship is exceptionally well established, catalogued, and digitized relative to more contested or emerging musicological topics elsewhere in the discipline. The foundational-scaffolding cap that held the rating to Medium at 24 months applies only at that horizon under this framework's rule, since the sequence-entry role matters most before students have progressed well past it into upper-level coursework. With no general studies designation applicable, the rating rises to High.

A decade out, under continued METR/Epoch-pace capability growth in research and analytical writing, this course's applied tasks, synthesizing historical and stylistic knowledge from scores and recordings spanning Ancient Greece through the Baroque, should be substantially reproducible by AI with limited expert correction, extending the 5-year trend further across the survey's full historical scope and analytical depth. The hedge here is about pedagogical rather than technical uncertainty: a foundational history-sequence course may be retained deliberately to build a shared knowledge base for majors regardless of whether AI can generate the same analysis, since the sequence's institutional function is architectural, not purely task-instrumental. No general studies designation and no further foundational cap apply at this later horizon, so the rating remains High.
MUS 3210.d: This course is intended for music majors. It comprises a comprehensive survey of Western music history and musical style through the examination of recordings and musical scores. This course traces the origins of Western music in Ancient Greek civilization, and explores the development of polyphony and rhythmic notation in the Middle Ages. An exploration of musical developments and ideas in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries of the Renaissance follows, and the course concludes with study of the musical Baroque era, spanning roughly 1600 to 1750.

r: Western Music History II asks majors to trace Classical, Romantic, and twentieth-century style through score analysis and primary-source reading, producing written interpretation of musical development. This work is textual and analytical rather than performative, sitting squarely inside the kind of writing and information-synthesis task that task-exposure research classifies as positively associated with AI exposure. Large models can already summarize period style, contextualize a composer against primary-source excerpts, and draft comparative analysis of scores in prose. Verification burden is moderate: music-historical claims are checkable against established scholarship, so errors are catchable rather than high-stakes. No general-studies designation or licensure mandate protects the course, and it is not a load-bearing prerequisite for many later requirements. At 24 months, students and instructors are only beginning to route routine score-context writing through AI tools, so the rating holds Medium rather than tipping higher immediately.

By 2031, AI models will produce fluent stylistic analysis, contextual essays, and score commentary comparable to competent undergraduate work, and observed-usage data already shows writing and information-synthesis tasks concentrated in exactly this kind of output. The course's central deliverable, connecting a score to its period's aesthetics and to secondary scholarship, is the type of bounded, well-documented task where AI performance is strong and adoption is no longer novel. Verification burden stays moderate rather than protective, since claims can be checked against a stable historical record, and full digital embodiment means nothing about the task resists automation on presence grounds. No general-studies or licensure lock caps the erosion, and the course is not deeply foundational scaffolding beyond its own two-course sequence. The rating rises to High, though how thoroughly programs will still require students to write analysis themselves remains an open pedagogical question.

A decade out, distinguishing AI-generated musicological writing from a student's own becomes harder to justify as a curricular rationale on task grounds alone; capability-trend evidence points to substantially longer and more reliable model task horizons by 2036, and diffusion, while historically uneven, tends to catch up over a decade. The instrumental case for requiring students to personally produce comparative stylistic analysis weakens further, since the underlying task, reading a score and primary sources and writing contextualized interpretation, is well within a fully digital, checkable domain. Absent an institutional lock or foundational role, nothing structurally protects the course from this trajectory. The rating holds High, with real uncertainty about pacing: adoption in Colorado humanities coursework depends on instructor practice and academic-integrity norms as much as on raw model capability, so the horizon is a directional call, not a confident point prediction.
MUS 3220.d: This course is intended for music majors. It comprises a comprehensive survey of Western music history and musical style through the examination of musical scores and primary and secondary source readings. This course traces the musical developments of the Classical era in the late eighteenth century, followed by a study of the development of musical style and aesthetics in the Romantic era of the nineteenth century. The course finishes with an overview of the radical musical developments of the twentieth century and considers new musical trends at the beginning of the twenty-first century.

r: This course has students compose original songs, lyrics, melody, harmony, and document them for performance across genres, building a personal songwriting method. Generative music tools already produce full songs with lyrics, melodic lines, and harmonic accompaniment across many styles, and task-exposure research finds writing and creative-composition tasks strongly positively associated with AI exposure, unlike science and critical-thinking work. Real-deliverable evaluation shows top models now reach roughly half of expert-level wins on occupational creative deliverables, closing in on parity. Verification burden is moderate rather than protective: judging a song's quality is subjective, not adversarial or safety-critical, so expert oversight is a craft preference rather than a hard requirement. The task is fully digital, notation, lyric drafting, and demoing can all happen without physical presence. No designation or accreditation floor protects the course, and it is not prerequisite scaffolding. The rating is High even at 24 months.

By 2031, AI song-generation systems will likely handle genre-specific composition, arrangement, and lyric-writing with more consistency, and observed-usage patterns already show substantial adoption of writing and office-style creative tasks in both consumer and enterprise settings. The course's core instrumental task, producing a documented, performable original song, increasingly overlaps with what generative tools do competently and are already deployed to do. What is harder for AI to replicate is the reflective articulation of one's own aesthetic method that the course also emphasizes, but the deliverable itself, the song, is squarely exposed. Moderate verification burden and full digital embodiment do not protect the course, and no general-studies or accreditation lock applies. The rating remains High, with the caveat that instructional emphasis may shift toward critiquing and directing AI-generated material rather than composing from a blank page.

Ten years out, distinguishing a human-composed song from a competently AI-generated one on craft grounds alone becomes increasingly difficult, and capability-trend evidence suggests substantially longer, more reliable model performance on creative, open-ended tasks by 2036. The instrumental rationale for a dedicated songwriting course increasingly rests on cultivating a personal aesthetic voice and critical judgment about generated material rather than on task performance the AI cannot match. Nothing in the course's institutional profile, no designation, no accreditation floor, no foundational role for later required courses, holds the rating down. The rating stays High, though this is a directional projection: how songwriting pedagogy actually adapts, and whether human-composed original work retains market or classroom value independent of AI competence, is genuinely uncertain over a ten-year horizon and not a confident point prediction.
MUS 3240.d: This course provides students with the basic aesthetic and communicative concepts of songwriting with regard to tradition and to contemporary trends and enables students to articulate a conscious method appropriate to their own aesthetic approaches to songwriting in the context of traditional songwriting. The course includes composing original songs with various features (lyrics, melody, harmony, etc.) and document them so that each song may be communicated and performed in various different genres, styles, and situations.

r: This course teaches IPA transcription for singing, vocal-instrument physiology, and practical instruction in vocal production, a psychomotor and physiological skill developed through guided, real-time practice. Task-exposure research consistently finds manual, physical, and in-person instructional work at the low end of AI exposure, and that holds here: a model can describe laryngeal physiology or transcribe IPA symbols, but it cannot listen to a student's tone, diagnose tension in the larynx, or physically shape breath support and resonance in real time. Verification burden is protective, incorrect technique advice risks vocal strain or injury, so a knowledgeable instructor must be present. Embodiment is also protective: vocal production is inseparable from the physical instrument. No accreditation floor caps the course, but neither factor needs it. The rating is Low, driven by task content rather than institutional lock.

By 2031, AI tools will likely give more sophisticated feedback on IPA accuracy and explain vocal physiology with more nuance, and some diagnostic pronunciation feedback may improve. But the jagged-frontier finding, that users relying on AI outside its competence zone perform meaningfully worse, with miscalibrated trust, is directly relevant to real-time vocal correction, where subtle physiological cues from breath, tension, and resonance are not text-legible. Verification burden and physical embodiment both remain protective, since a mis-corrected vocal habit compounds over time and is hard to reverse. The instrumental need for a human pedagogue who can hear and physically guide the student holds. The rating stays Low, with modest movement plausible only in the surrounding theoretical content, not in the applied vocal-production core.

A decade out, some audio-analysis tools may plausibly assist with real-time pitch, formant, or pronunciation feedback, narrowing the diagnostic gap somewhat. But the course's central task, training a human ear and a human instructor's physical judgment to shape another person's voice safely, remains embodied and high-stakes in a way that task-exposure research and the jagged-frontier finding both suggest resists full substitution. Capability trends point to faster and more capable models generally, but capability alone does not eliminate the need for in-person physiological correction of a live, individual instrument, since vocal injury from mishandled technique is a real and lasting cost. The rating holds Low, acknowledging real uncertainty about how much technological mediation enters voice pedagogy by 2036, without predicting that the embodied instructional core is eliminated or that a human instructor becomes optional.
MUS 3250.d: This course covers use of the International Phonetic Alphabet and associated sounds for singing in English and other commonly sung languages as well as physiology of the human vocal instrument and practical instruction for vocal production.

r: This course builds resumes, cover letters, interview skills, networking practice, personal-finance basics, contract negotiation, and marketing strategy for musicians, almost entirely writing, research, and communication tasks. Observed-usage data already shows writing and office-style tasks concentrated among the most common AI uses, and drafting resumes, cover letters, and marketing plans is a mainstream application today, not a speculative one. Professional-writing productivity research finds AI assistance cutting drafting time substantially while improving output quality, with the largest gains for less experienced writers, a strong match for students producing career documents for the first time. Verification burden is moderate: a bad negotiating clause or financial assumption carries real cost, so some human judgment remains necessary, but the informational core is checkable. No designation or accreditation floor protects the course. The rating is High even at 24 months, reflecting task content already well inside AI's competence.

By 2031, AI career-coaching tools will likely be more integrated and personalized, handling resume tailoring, interview rehearsal, and market-niche research with less need for a dedicated course to teach the mechanics. Observed-usage patterns already skew toward automation rather than augmentation for consumer writing tasks, and that trend plausibly deepens for templated professional documents. What resists automation is the applied judgment behind negotiating a real contract or evaluating a genuinely dubious opportunity, where verification burden remains real. Nothing about the course's content is physically embodied, and no institutional lock protects it. The rating stays High, with the caveat that career-development curricula may pivot toward directing and evaluating AI-generated materials and toward higher-stakes negotiation judgment rather than mechanics like formatting a resume.

Ten years out, generic career-document production, resumes, cover letters, standard marketing copy, is a plausible candidate for near-complete AI handling, consistent with capability-trend projections of longer and more reliable task performance and with writing's strong positive association with exposure in task-exposure research. The instrumental case for a dedicated course likely narrows toward negotiation judgment, personal-finance decision-making, and networking, which retain a human-judgment and relational component AI does not fully substitute. No accreditation or foundational-role protection exists to hold the course in place structurally, and diffusion evidence suggests adoption of these tools among students will be widespread well before 2036. The rating holds High, though this projects a clear directional trend rather than a confident claim about exactly which career-development tasks remain manual by 2036.
MUS 3260.d: This course offers a foundation upon which students can develop the musical careers they seek and provides firsthand experience with a few of the basic tools all modern musicians need to succeed, including: resume and cover letter writing, interviewing, networking, personal finance management, negotiating contracts, establishing a strong work ethic, developing marketing strategies, and identifying market niches they can fill. Students practice and apply skills through course activities, both in-classroom and online, providing a bridge to their professional career.

r: This course develops competencies for teaching elementary and secondary general music: traditional methodologies, technology integration, non-ensemble musical activities, classroom management, and assessment strategy, feeding directly into the paired supervised field experience. Classroom management and real-time instructional judgment with children are interpersonal and in-person by nature, which task-exposure research treats as low-exposure territory even as it flags programmatic and writing tasks as more exposed. AI can help draft lesson plans or assessment rubrics, but the course's applied core, managing a live classroom of P-12 students, is not something a model performs. Verification burden is protective, since misapplied classroom-management or assessment approaches affect real children's learning. The course also contributes to the music-education licensure sequence, a partial institutional constraint. The rating is Low, reflecting task content: the embodied instructional core outweighs the more exposed planning-and-assessment-design components.

By 2031, AI-assisted lesson planning, differentiated-materials generation, and assessment design will likely be well integrated into music-teacher preparation, eroding the informational and planning components of this course. But classroom management and live pedagogical judgment with elementary and secondary students remain embodied, real-time, and interpersonal, squarely outside what task-exposure research or productivity studies describe as strong AI territory. Verification burden stays protective: a teacher-candidate learning to read a room of children needs a human mentor's calibrated feedback, not just AI-generated technique advice, since misapplied classroom strategy has direct consequences for student learning. The course's contribution to the licensure sequence remains a partial institutional anchor. The rating stays Low, with the acknowledgment that the planning-and-technology half of the course content is trending toward augmentation, even as the classroom-management half resists it.

A decade out, AI-generated lesson content, assessment strategies, and technology-integration guidance are plausibly routine inputs to teacher preparation, consistent with capability-trend projections of much longer effective task horizons by 2036. The instrumental rationale for the course increasingly concentrates on the irreducibly human classroom-management and real-time pedagogical-judgment components rather than on materials design, which shifts the balance upward from Low. The music-education licensure sequence continues to anchor the course institutionally as contributory credit, capping how far the rating can move even as the underlying planning tasks become substantially AI-mediated. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting a directional shift toward AI handling more of the planning workload while human classroom presence remains necessary, a projection carrying real uncertainty about how teacher-prep programs restructure this content by 2036.
MUS 3350.d: Students develop competencies for teaching general music in both elementary and secondary school music settings. Course content includes experience with traditional elementary methodologies, application of technology to music, and non- ensemble based musical opportunities. Additional instruction includes classroom management, assessment strategies, and the role of general music in education.

r: This course places students in area elementary schools for a 55-hour supervised field experience, integrating general-music teaching methods with live practice under a supervising teacher. The task is maximally embodied and interpersonal: standing in front of real children, adapting instruction in real time, and being evaluated by a human mentor on demonstrated classroom competence. Task-exposure research places this kind of in-person, physically present instructional work at the low end of exposure, in contrast to the writing and programming tasks it identifies as most exposed. Verification burden is at its most protective here, a teacher-candidate's readiness for licensure must be judged by a qualified human observer in an actual classroom, not inferred from AI-generated material. The clock-hour field-experience structure functions as a hard, course-specific institutional mandate, similar to clinical or practicum requirements elsewhere. The rating is Low, with essentially no ambiguity.

By 2031, AI tools may assist a teacher-candidate's lesson preparation before entering the classroom, but the field-experience task itself, physically present, supervised teaching of children, evaluated hour by hour, does not change in kind. Embodiment and verification burden remain maximally protective: licensure readiness has to be observed and certified by a human supervisor watching real instruction, not simulated. The 55-hour clock-hour structure continues to function as a hard institutional mandate tying the course to a specific requirement rather than a general credit total. Capability trends point to more powerful models generally, but supervised clinical placement is precisely the kind of requirement that institutional and licensure mandates hold in place regardless of underlying AI capability. The rating stays Low, with little expected movement even as adjacent planning tasks shift toward AI assistance.

Ten years out, the structural logic protecting this course, physical presence, human supervision, and a fixed clock-hour requirement, is unlikely to be substantially disrupted by AI capability growth alone, since diffusion evidence shows institutional and licensure structures changing far more slowly than model capability. Remote or simulated teaching-practice tools might supplement preparation, but a supervised field placement with a human evaluator remains the operative requirement for licensure pathways in this model, and no reasonably foreseeable regulatory change removes that clock-hour anchor. The rating holds Low, reflecting sustained confidence in the embodied, supervised, clock-hour-anchored nature of the task rather than a prediction that no AI-assisted teacher-preparation tools will exist by 2036, they likely will, just not as a substitute for this course's core requirement.
MUS 3351.d: The student works with elementary general music teachers in area schools in a 55-hour supervised field experience. The course is designed to integrate concepts developed in MUS 3350 with practice in classroom environments.

r: This course builds hands-on playing skill on classroom instruments, barred and non-pitched percussion, drums, recorder, guitar, and ukulele, so future teachers can model and lead performance in a P-12 general-music classroom. The task is psychomotor: developing finger technique, rhythm, and instrumental fluency through repeated physical practice, which task-exposure research places firmly outside the writing and programming activities it identifies as most AI-exposed. An AI system can supply fingering charts or rhythm notation, but it cannot develop a student's own manual dexterity or ensemble timing. Verification burden is moderate, an instructor corrects technique through demonstration and listening, a fundamentally in-person process. No designation or accreditation floor applies, and none is needed given how firmly embodied the task is. The rating is Low, grounded in the physical nature of instrumental skill-building rather than any institutional protection.

By 2031, instructional apps and AI-assisted practice tools may offer more refined feedback on rhythm accuracy or fingering, but they still cannot substitute for a teacher-candidate physically learning to play barred percussion, guitar, or recorder well enough to model it live for children. Embodiment remains sharply protective: this is motor-skill acquisition, not information retrieval, and the jagged-frontier concern about AI users overestimating unfamiliar-domain performance argues against trusting text-based guidance for hands-on technique. Verification burden stays moderate rather than becoming a major driver, since the binding constraint here is physical presence, not oversight cost. No institutional lock is needed to hold the course in place. The rating remains Low, with only the surrounding theoretical content, not the playing skill itself, plausibly touched by AI tools.

A decade out, capability-trend projections point to more capable and more embedded AI tools generally, potentially including more sophisticated practice-feedback apps for classroom instruments. But acquiring physical instrumental competence, the ability to actually play barred percussion, guitar, ukulele, and recorder well enough to teach children, remains a psychomotor skill that a teacher-candidate must personally hold, not one an AI system can perform on their behalf, no matter how fluent its text-based instruction becomes. Task-exposure research's consistent finding that manual and physical work sits at the low end of exposure supports continued protection here. The rating holds Low, acknowledging genuine uncertainty about how digital practice tools reshape the surrounding pedagogy, but not projecting that hands-on instrumental skill-building becomes instrumentally unnecessary by 2036.
MUS 3360.d: Students develop practical skills in playing instruments typically used in the P-12 general music class. These instruments include, but are not limited to barred percussion instruments, non- pitched percussion, drums, recorder, guitar, and ukulele.

r: This course surveys exceptionalities across the P-12 spectrum, covers child abuse and medical-condition indicators, and builds strategies and curriculum adaptations for inclusive music and art classrooms. AI can help draft differentiated materials or summarize disability categories, a task-exposed activity, but the course's core purpose is developing a teacher-candidate's own judgment about a specific child in front of them, recognizing abuse indicators, weighing a medical condition's classroom implications, applying special-education processes correctly. Verification burden is strongly protective: misjudging a disclosure or an adaptation carries real welfare consequences for a child, exactly the high-error-cost, non-obvious-failure scenario the framework treats as requiring a knowledgeable human. The course contributes to the music-education licensure sequence as a partial institutional anchor. The rating is Low, driven primarily by verification burden rather than by task content alone.

By 2031, AI tools may generate competent draft adaptations or summarize special-education frameworks more fluently, chipping at the informational surface of this content. But the jagged-frontier finding, that AI users outside the model's reliable competence zone perform meaningfully worse while trusting the output more, is directly relevant to safeguarding judgments and individualized adaptation decisions, where errors are not always obvious and stakes are high. Verification burden remains the dominant protective factor: a teacher-candidate must personally develop the judgment to apply inclusion strategies and recognize welfare concerns correctly, not defer to generated text. The licensure-sequence contribution continues to anchor the course institutionally. The rating stays Low, with the caveat that supporting materials generation is the part most likely to shift toward AI assistance.

A decade out, AI systems will likely be far more capable at explaining special-education frameworks and drafting differentiated content, consistent with capability-trend projections of longer and more reliable task performance. But the course's central instrumental purpose, a teacher-candidate developing personal, real-time judgment about vulnerable children's welfare and instructional needs, remains a high-verification-burden task that the framework treats as resistant to substitution regardless of model capability, since the cost of an uncaught error falls on a child and is not always visible until after harm occurs. The licensure-sequence anchor persists as a partial institutional constraint. The rating holds Low, reflecting sustained confidence in the protective role of verification burden here rather than a claim that AI plays no role in inclusive-classroom preparation by 2036.
MUS 3390.d: This course provides a survey of various exceptionalities of K-12 students, ranging from mild to severe, with a focus on meeting the needs of these students in the music classroom. Information about child abuse and medical conditions, and their possible effects on student learning and behavior, is addressed. Teacher-candidates are introduced to special education processes with music content that facilitates the learning process of students with special needs, including strategies and curriculum adaptations for inclusion in music and art classrooms.

r: This advanced course trains German and French vowel and consonant pronunciation for classical singing, demonstrated in live class performances and presentations. The task is embodied performance: shaping breath, articulation, and resonance to produce accurate sung diction in a foreign language, evaluated by listening in real time. Task-exposure research is consistent on this point, manual, physical, and performative activity sits at the low end of AI exposure, distinct from the writing and programming tasks it flags as most automatable. But the central case still requires a human conductor physically in front of a choir, reading vocal production and ensemble balance moment to moment and adjusting gesture accordingly — an embodied, real-time interpersonal task with no AI substitute. r: MUS 3650 teaches the craft of musical composition, practical technique, theory application, and aesthetic judgment, developed by writing individual pieces and presenting them for critique and performance in a workshop setting. Because composition here is a notated, largely digital activity produced outside class and reviewed in discussion rather than live ensemble performance, embodiment offers only partial protection. Still, verification of a composition's aesthetic and technical success, voice-leading, orchestration, formal coherence, is not something a student can outsource without expert judgment, and the course sits within an NASM-accredited composition sequence and precedes private-instruction coursework. At 24 months the instrumental need to personally develop compositional craft is not yet eroded.

By 2031, generative-music systems will draft stylistically competent compositions on demand, and professional-writing productivity research already shows large time savings alongside quality gains when AI assists composition-adjacent writing tasks, a pattern likely to extend to notated music. That erodes the produce-the-piece-yourself rationale somewhat, but the workshop model's core deliverable is a discussion-and-performance critique of the student's own craft decisions, and misjudging AI-generated material's coherence carries real verification cost for an inexperienced composer, per jagged-frontier findings on miscalibrated trust outside a model's reliable range. The course also remains a prerequisite substrate feeding private-composition instruction later in the sequence. On balance the instrumental case still favors personal skill-building, but exposure is rising quickly. The rating holds Low, near the boundary, reflecting genuine erosion pressure on the underlying composing task.

A decade out, AI composition tools will plausibly generate full, well-crafted pieces across genres with modest prompting, substantially eroding the rationale that a student must personally produce compositional drafts to learn the craft. GDPval-style evaluations suggest near-parity, not full parity, on real creative deliverables, leaving a residual role for trained aesthetic judgment and revision that the course cultivates. Ten years out, under substantial uncertainty about how generative video and audio reshape opera production and the broader performing-arts economy, the specific task this course builds, a student physically singing and acting an operatic role live alongside a cast, remains one AI does not perform on the student's behalf. Capability trends point toward far more convincing synthetic performance media by 2036, which is primarily an industry and labor-market question this rating excludes rather than an instrumental one for a student learning to stage a role. The most plausible change is in how supporting materials like translations, historical context, or character research are prepared, not in whether staged rehearsal and live performance remain required. The rating holds Low, with the caveat that the professional opera and screen-performance markets surrounding this training are considerably more exposed than the course's instrumental necessity.
MUS 3833.d: This course is designed to prepare students for a performance of a full-length opera or opera scenes. Students receive coaching and direction on all assigned material. In addition, students may take part in exercises which may increase their abilities to develop natural stage movements appropriate to their operatic characters. Students fill out a character profile form for each of their assigned roles. This ensemble is open to all students who successfully pass the audition.

r: This non-auditioned, open-enrollment course introduces students, with no prior musical experience required, to Balinese gamelan angklung technique and repertoire through hands-on participation culminating in an evening performance. The applied work is embodied and orally transmitted: learning interlocking rhythmic patterns and ensemble listening by directly playing provided instruments alongside an instructor and peers, a mode of cultural and musical knowledge transmission that task-exposure research does not classify as automatable, unlike the writing and computational tasks dominating current AI use. The binding constraint is presence: gamelan performance depends on tight rhythmic interlock among performers that can only be built through repeated shared physical rehearsal, and an instructor's live correction of timing and technique cannot be replicated remotely. The course is open enrollment with no prerequisite gatekeeping. At 24 months, the instrumental need to physically learn this tradition through participation is essentially unchanged.

By 2031, AI systems will likely generate convincing gamelan-style audio or notate the interlocking parts more accessibly, but observed-usage data shows AI activity concentrated in computational and office work rather than displacing embodied musical participation, and generating a recording is a different task from a student learning to play the interlocking patterns live with an ensemble. The instrumental case for the course, developing the aural and physical skill to perform this tradition in coordination with others, is unchanged: verification of tight ensemble timing requires an instructor listening in the room, and a recording or transcription cannot substitute for the shared physical practice. Across a catalog cycle the participatory, no-prerequisite ensemble format holds, and its contributory role toward NASM-adjacent ensemble expectations reinforces the floor. The rating stays Low.

A decade out, under considerable uncertainty about how generative audio tools intersect with traditional and world-music pedagogy, the specific task this course builds, learning to physically perform interlocking Balinese gamelan patterns as part of a live ensemble, remains outside what AI executes on a student's behalf; the cultural and embodied transmission is the substance of the course. Capability trends suggest AI-generated approximations of the style will be far more convincing by 2036, but a course whose stated purpose is participatory experience of the tradition does not have an instrumental substitute in synthetic audio. The most plausible ten-year change is in supplementary materials or recordings used for study, not in whether hands-on ensemble participation remains the course's core activity. The rating holds Low.
MUS 3834.d: The Gamelan Ensemble provides students with the opportunity to experience traditional Balinese gamelan music through participation and performance. Students are introduced to basic techniques and repertoire on a Balinese gamelan angklung. The semester culminates in an evening performance. No prior musical experience is necessary, and instruments will be provided in class. It is a non-auditioned ensemble and open to all students regardless of their major.

r: This non-auditioned, open-enrollment ensemble introduces students, with no previous musical experience required, to African and African-diasporic drumming and dance traditions through direct participation, developing technique in both drumming and movement toward an end-of-semester performance. The applied work combines psychomotor drumming technique with embodied dance, both real-time, physically demanding, and traditionally transmitted through direct instructor modeling and group practice, activities task-exposure research places well outside AI's currently automatable range in contrast to writing and computational work. The binding constraint is embodiment across two simultaneous physical disciplines: rhythm production on drums and coordinated movement, both requiring an instructor's live physical correction and repeated group rehearsal that cannot occur without shared physical presence. The course carries no prerequisite and is open to any student. At 24 months, the instrumental need to build these embodied skills through direct participation is essentially unchanged by AI capability elsewhere.

By 2031, AI tools may generate audio approximations of African drumming rhythms or provide reference recordings, but observed-usage data shows AI activity concentrated in Computer and Mathematical and office-style work, not in delivering embodied physical instruction, and a generated rhythm track does not teach a student the drumming technique or dance vocabulary this course builds through direct modeling. The instrumental case is unchanged: verification of correct drumming technique and dance coordination requires an instructor physically present to observe and correct posture, timing, and movement in real time. Across a catalog cycle the hands-on, no-prerequisite participatory format holds, and the course's contributory role toward NASM-adjacent ensemble and cultural-performance expectations reinforces that floor. The rating stays Low; reference recordings may supplement study but do not replace embodied instruction.

Ten years out, under considerable uncertainty about how AI-generated media intersects with traditional cultural performance pedagogy, the dual embodied core of this course, drumming technique and dance movement learned through direct participation, is not a task a model performs on a student's behalf. Capability trends point to increasingly convincing synthetic audio and even generated movement demonstrations by 2036, but a course built around direct cultural transmission and physical skill development retains its instrumental rationale precisely because the learning is the embodied doing, not the consumption of a reference artifact. The most plausible ten-year change is in supplementary study materials rather than in whether hands-on group participation remains necessary. The rating holds Low, with the standard hedge that how such traditions are taught and documented may evolve well before this instrumental requirement does.
MUS 3835.d: This ensemble introduces the varied and rich musical traditions of Africa and the African diasporas through participation and performance. The course focuses on the development of a variety of drumming and dance techniques, while cultivating a program of pieces for performance at the end of the semester. No previous musical experience is required, and it is a non-auditioned ensemble and open to all students regardless of their major.

r: Pop and Soul Choir develops group vocal performance: blend, harmony singing, dynamics, phrasing, vocal health, and group dynamics, cultivated through real-time rehearsal under an instructor's ear. The applied work is physical and interpersonal, coordinating multiple singers into a unified live sound, a psychomotor and social activity rather than a written or analytical deliverable. Task-exposure research classifies manual, physical, real-time interpersonal work as low-exposure, in sharp contrast to the writing and programming tasks it flags as strongly positively associated with automation. Generative vocal-synthesis tools can already produce convincing layered vocal tracks, but nothing substitutes for a student learning to blend their own voice with peers in a room. At 24 months there is no meaningful erosion: verifying blend, tuning, and dynamics still requires a trained human ear present during rehearsal, and no designation locks the course beyond that embodied necessity.

By 2031, AI vocal tools will be markedly more capable at generating stylistically convincing harmony arrangements and reference vocal tracks, and some students may use them to explore blend choices before rehearsal. That shifts practice methods but not the instrumental need: the course still requires students to physically produce, tune, and blend live vocal parts in real time with an ensemble, a psychomotor skill no model performs on the learner's behalf. Verification burden stays protective because judging live blend and dynamics against peers demands an in-room human ear; the jagged-frontier finding that AI users misjudge quality outside a model's true competence applies directly to unsupervised vocal-arrangement generation. No general-studies or accreditation lock exists here, but none is needed: embodiment alone keeps the rating anchored. The rating holds Low, with the caveat that pre-rehearsal preparation tools will keep expanding around the edges of the course.

A decade out, synthetic vocal production will be pervasive across the commercial music economy, and ensembles may rehearse against AI-generated reference tracks routinely. Even so, the specific competence Pop and Soul Choir builds is the embodied act of singing in blend with other people in real time, which remains outside what a generative model executes for the student. The central case under wide uncertainty still has vocal ensemble courses run as in-person rehearsal because the skill is definitionally psychomotor and interpersonal, not informational. The more plausible ten-year shift is in the commercial vocal-production labor market surrounding graduates, not in whether learning to sing in an ensemble requires doing it. The rating stays Low; the honest hedge is that AI's role in shaping repertoire, arrangements, and reference tracks around the course is far less certain than the embodied-skill rationale itself.
MUS 3836.d: This ensemble class focuses on singing in a group setting, teaching students primarily about vocal technique, vocal health, vocal blend, harmony singing, dynamics, phrasing, and group dynamics. This class includes repertoire ranging from contemporary popular music to classic soul.

r: Live Performance Workshop trains students to play live on-stage with professional equipment, developing musical communication, performance ability, stage presence, and sound design through modeled feedback from instructors during actual live sessions. The applied work is real-time psychomotor execution and interpersonal stage communication, activities task-exposure research does not classify among the automatable range it reserves for writing, coding, and administrative-style tasks. Sound design has digital components, but the course centers on the embodied act of performing live with a band under instructor observation, not on producing a discrete artifact AI could substitute. At 24 months, no erosion is evident: the instrumental need is the student's own stage presence and live musicianship, built through repeated performance that cannot be delegated to a model. The course also feeds directly into Group Recital, giving it a modest scaffolding role within the performance sequence.

By 2031, AI-assisted stage and sound-design tools will likely be more integrated into live production workflows, and students may rehearse against AI-generated backing tracks or use software for mix and monitor decisions. That changes the tools around the course, not its core instrumental task: developing a performer's stage presence, timing, and live musical communication in front of an instructor and peers. Verification burden stays protective because assessing stage presence and live musical judgment requires a human evaluator physically present; the jagged-frontier evidence on miscalibrated trust outside a model's competence is especially relevant to unsupervised live-performance feedback. No general-studies or accreditation designation constrains the course, but embodiment alone is sufficient to hold the rating. The course's minor prerequisite role for Group Recital adds a small further reason the applied-study sequence persists across a catalog cycle.

Under a wide-uncertainty ten-year view, AI-generated live-adjacent media (synthetic performers, virtual production) will be far more capable and could reshape parts of the commercial live-music industry. That is a labor-market question outside this rating's scope. The instrumental question — whether a student needs to personally practice performing live, on stage, under real equipment and real-time feedback — remains essentially unchanged, because stage presence and live musical communication are embodied competencies that a model does not develop on the student's behalf. The most plausible shift by 2036 is in the technology surrounding live shows (automated sound design, AI-assisted lighting and mixing) rather than in whether the performer's own live craft must still be built through practice. The rating holds Low, with real but bounded uncertainty about how much of the surrounding production toolchain becomes automated.
MUS 3840.d: This course prepares students to play live, on-stage with professional equipment to the highest musical standards. Students perform in various live group sessions in which musical communication, performance ability, stage presence, and sound design are modeled by instructors who will provide feedback. This course can be repeated for credit.

r: Commercial Composition and Arranging has students apply techniques and methodologies to compose and arrange original music, and analyze classic and contemporary songs through score analysis and critical listening. These are digital, notation- and audio-based tasks: producing arrangements, annotating scores, and writing analytical assessments. Observed-usage data already shows Computer & Mathematical work as the largest category of AI use, and current generative-music and notation-assist tools can draft plausible arrangements and stylistic analyses today. At 24 months, AI-assisted arranging is realized but not yet the default professional workflow, and a trained ear is still needed to judge voicing, balance, and idiomatic fit, keeping the course's instrumental need only moderately eroded. No general-studies designation or accreditation mandate protects the course, and it is not a prerequisite bottleneck for later required courses, so nothing structurally caps the rating.

By 2031, generative composition and arranging tools will plausibly handle a substantial share of routine arranging tasks — voicing chord changes, adapting a song across instrumentation, producing stylistically consistent drafts — at a level approaching commercial usability, consistent with the capability trend of rapidly lengthening task-time horizons. Task-exposure research already associates writing- and composition-adjacent tasks with high automation exposure, and score analysis and critical-listening writeups are squarely writing-like deliverables. Verification burden is moderate rather than strictly protective: arrangement choices are correctable and low-stakes compared to adversarial or safety-critical work, so expert review, while valuable, is not an absolute constraint on deployment. With no institutional lock-in and no foundational-prerequisite role, the rating rises to High: the course's core applied tasks are increasingly ones AI can competently perform and that the field is plausibly adopting.

A decade out, under wide capability and adoption uncertainty, AI arranging and composition tools are plausibly commonplace across commercial music production, handling much of the mechanical work of arranging a song for a given ensemble or style. The course's analytical and score-analysis components are similarly exposed, since AI-generated musical analysis is already improving quickly. The countervailing consideration is that human arrangers still curate, direct, and make final aesthetic judgments, and macro-level productivity effects from AI diffusion have historically been modest even as capability grows, so full automation of professional arranging work is not a safe assumption. Still, absent any institutional lock or foundational role protecting this specific course, the central case keeps the rating High, with the caveat that the balance between AI-assisted drafting and human arranging judgment ten years out is genuinely uncertain.
MUS 3850.d: This course requires that students study and apply techniques, methodologies, and concepts for composing and arranging original music. Students analyze classic and contemporary songs and arrangements, including score analysis and critical listening assessments.

r: Live Songwriting Workshop has students write original songs to professional standards in small groups, applying songwriting methodologies and lyric-writing techniques to genre-specific briefs while analyzing published songwriters' creative processes. Lyric writing and song-structure work are text-generation tasks squarely inside what task-exposure research flags as strongly positively associated with automation, and current generative-lyric and melody tools can already produce usable drafts against a brief. At 24 months, students and working songwriters increasingly use AI for first drafts, rhyme and structure suggestions, and genre-matching, though the group-collaboration and specific-brief-fulfillment aspects still benefit from human creative judgment and taste, keeping the erosion moderate rather than complete. No general-studies designation or accreditation credit-hour mandate applies, and the course is not a required prerequisite substrate for later coursework, so nothing structurally caps the rating below what the task content supports.

By 2031, AI songwriting tools will plausibly generate full draft songs — lyrics, melody, and structure — matched to a stated brief and genre at a level much closer to professional usability, consistent with rapidly lengthening AI task-time horizons. Professional-writing productivity research already documents large time savings alongside quality gains when writers use AI assistance, a pattern directly applicable to lyric drafting and revision. The workshop's small-group, brief-driven format is exactly the kind of writing task that benefits from such tools, and verification burden is moderate rather than strictly protective, since a flawed AI-drafted lyric is a correctable creative artifact rather than a high-stakes error. With no institutional lock-in and no foundational role in the curriculum, the rating rises to High: the instrumental need for a student to personally generate every draft is substantially reduced, even as originality and taste remain contested territory.

Ten years out, under considerable uncertainty about both capability and diffusion, AI songwriting assistance is plausibly a standard part of commercial songwriting workflows, handling much of the drafting labor the workshop currently assigns to students working in small groups. The countervailing evidence is that adoption has historically lagged capability, and creative differentiation — a songwriter's distinctive voice, judgment about audience and genre nuance — is precisely the kind of ambiguous, low-verification-burden output that even capable models struggle to be trusted with unsupervised. Given no institutional lock protecting this specific course and no foundational-prerequisite role, the central case still points to High, while acknowledging real uncertainty about whether songwriting pedagogy shifts toward curating and directing AI drafts rather than eliminating the writing task outright.
MUS 3860.d: Within this course, students develop original songs to a professional standard. Students work in small groups, writing several songs to specific briefs; thus, students put into practice various songwriting methodologies and lyric writing techniques. Students also analyze the work of various professional songwriters to gain a better understanding of their creative processes. Emphasis is placed on understanding the qualities of specific genres and writing to those specifications.

r: Advanced Songwriting has students deconstruct a challenging set of songs for melodic, harmonic, rhythmic, formal, and lyrical qualities, building theoretical knowledge, music literacy, and aural skills, then produce original material across a range of prompts, styles, and genres while reflecting on their own practice. This blends writing-like lyric and structural tasks, which task-exposure research associates with high automation exposure, against deeper theoretical and aural-skills analysis, a domain the same research associates with lower exposure because it resembles critical-thinking work.
