At 24 months, current tools handle surface-level lyric and structure drafting reasonably well but are weaker at the layered melodic-harmonic-formal analysis and genre-transcending synthesis this advanced course demands, keeping realized automatability modest. The course carries no general-studies designation and is not a prerequisite for further required coursework, so its rating rests on task content alone.

By 2031, generative tools will plausibly handle both the lyric-writing and much of the melodic-harmonic-formal analysis this course requires, consistent with the capability trend of rapidly lengthening AI task-time horizons; drafting original material across multiple genres and prompts is a task profile increasingly within reach of frontier models. Verification burden remains moderate: judging whether a song genuinely transcends genre boundaries or reflects a student's own reflective practice is a correctable, low-stakes creative judgment rather than one demanding strict expert gatekeeping. With no institutional lock-in and no foundational-prerequisite role protecting the course, the rating rises to Medium as the balance shifts from human-only deep analysis toward AI-assisted synthesis, while the course's emphasis on personal aural-skills development and reflective practice still anchors a meaningful, if shrinking, human-only core.

A decade out, under wide uncertainty, AI systems plausibly perform sophisticated multi-dimensional song analysis and generate stylistically diverse original material competently, eroding much of the course's advanced-analysis and composition rationale. The countervailing factor is that task-exposure research still separates critical-thinking-heavy analytical work from purely generative writing, and this course's aural-skills and theoretical-literacy components sit closer to that more resistant category, so full erosion is not guaranteed. Absent any general-studies designation or foundational-prerequisite role to cap the rating, the central case moves to High, reflecting substantial realized automatability of both the analytical and compositional tasks by 2036, with the explicit caveat that how much of a songwriter's personal theoretical literacy remains instrumentally necessary once AI can perform equivalent analysis is genuinely unresolved.
MUS 3862.d: Building on Foundations of Songwriting, this course examines more advanced methods, techniques, and practices of the songwriting craft. Students deconstruct a more challenging set of songs to analyze their melodic, harmonic, rhythmic, formal, and lyrical qualities. Students continue to build their theoretical knowledge of music as well as their music literacy and aural skills. Using the knowledge gained through this analysis, students are asked to produce original material that expresses their uniqueness as songwriters as they work within a number of prompts that encourage them to write in a plethora of styles and genres, as well as transcending traditional genre boundaries. Students also reflect on their songwriting practices and style.

r: Commercial Electronic Music has students use programming, loops, samples, synthesis, MIDI, and multiple DAWs alongside classic and contemporary hardware to create original electronic compositions, producing several finished pieces through these tools. This is entirely digital, computer-mediated work, the category observed-usage data identifies as the largest share of current AI use, and generative-audio plugins already integrated into major DAWs can produce loops, stems, and stylistic variations on request. At 24 months, students and producers are realistically incorporating AI-assisted sound generation and arrangement suggestions into workflows resembling coding-assistant productivity gains documented elsewhere, though full compositions built entirely by AI to a specific creative brief are not yet the default. No general-studies designation applies, and the course sits outside any accreditation-credit mandate, so the rating reflects task exposure directly.

By 2031, AI-native music-production tools will plausibly be standard components of commercial electronic-music workflows, generating loops, synthesizer patches, and full draft arrangements at a level of competence approaching current coding-assistant productivity gains, consistent with rapidly lengthening AI task-time horizons. The course's task profile — technical, software-mediated, iterative production — is exactly the kind of work such tools accelerate most. Verification burden is moderate rather than protective, since a flawed AI-generated loop or patch is a low-stakes, correctable creative choice rather than a high-error-cost failure. With no institutional lock-in and no foundational-prerequisite role in the broader curriculum, the rating rises to High: the instrumental need for a student to manually construct every element of an electronic composition is substantially reduced by tools already diffusing into commercial practice.

Ten years out, under considerable uncertainty, AI music-production tools are plausibly deeply embedded in electronic-music creation, capable of generating full stylistically coherent compositions from prompts, which would substantially erode the instrumental need to manually operate every DAW, synthesis, and MIDI tool this course teaches. The countervailing consideration is that adoption has historically lagged raw capability, and producers may still need hands-on technical fluency to direct, edit, and integrate AI-generated material into a coherent creative vision, especially where hardware synthesis and live-tool integration require judgment a prompt-only workflow does not supply. Absent any general-studies designation or foundational role protecting the course, and with no accreditation credit-hour mandate to fall back on, the central case holds at High, while acknowledging genuine uncertainty about whether electronic-music pedagogy shifts toward directing and curating AI-generated material rather than eliminating hands-on production skill entirely.
MUS 3870.d: This course introduces students to the basic components and processes involved in creating original music by using contemporary electronic software and hardware. Students examine and learn to use programming, loops, samples, synthesis, MIDI, various DAWs (Digital Audio Workstations) as well as various contemporary and classic hardware tools used regularly to compose electronic music. Students are required to create multiple compositions by integrating a range of electronic music tools, techniques, and methodologies.

r: Group Recital builds on Live Performance Workshop by having students continue developing technical and improvisational skill on their instrument while also taking on musical-director responsibilities: forming and managing their own ensemble, choosing repertoire, cultivating a group sound, and ultimately constructing and performing a live set for an audience with faculty mentorship and feedback. The core applied work is embodied live performance plus real-time interpersonal leadership of a band, activities task-exposure research does not place among automatable tasks, unlike the writing and coding work it flags as exposed. AI tools can suggest repertoire or generate reference tracks, but they cannot rehearse, direct, or perform with a live ensemble on a student's behalf. At 24 months, the instrumental need is unchanged: mentored, in-person ensemble leadership and live performance remain the substance of the course.

By 2031, AI-assisted repertoire selection, arrangement drafting, and reference-track generation will likely be more common inputs into how a student-led ensemble prepares, but the course's actual applied work — rehearsing a band, cultivating a live group sound, and performing a set before an audience under mentor feedback — remains an embodied, real-time activity that a model does not perform for the student. Verification burden stays protective because faculty mentors judge live ensemble cohesion and performance quality in person, and the jagged-frontier finding on miscalibrated trust outside a model's true competence is directly relevant to any unsupervised reliance on AI-generated musical-direction advice. No general-studies or accreditation lock is needed to hold this course Low; embodiment and real-time leadership do that work on their own across a catalog cycle.

Under a wide-uncertainty ten-year view, AI will likely shape more of the surrounding commercial ensemble ecosystem — repertoire discovery, promotional material, even rehearsal-support tools — but the specific competence Group Recital builds, mentored live musical direction and ensemble performance, is not a task a model executes on the student's behalf. The central case still has this course run as in-person, mentor-guided ensemble work because the skills are definitionally psychomotor, interpersonal, and leadership-based rather than informational. The more plausible ten-year change is in the tools students use to prepare and promote their recitals, not in whether directing and performing with a live band requires doing it. The rating holds Low, with the caveat that the commercial context surrounding student ensembles is considerably more exposed than the pedagogical core.
MUS 3878.d: Building on Live Performance Workshop (MUS 3840), this class takes a more advanced approach to live performance. While continuing to develop technical and improvisational skills on their chosen instrument, students develop their skills as Musical Directors as they form and manage their own ensembles. Students choose repertoire as they cultivate a group sound and personality. Faculty offer feedback and constructive guidance to help mold a band into a cohesive professional unit. Various faculty members are assigned to each group as mentors. Each ensemble is responsible for constructing and performing a set for an audience of their peers and instructors, receiving feedback from both.

r: The Politics of Artists and Repertoire has students examine the history of A&R and record labels, focusing on backroom negotiations and deal-making through case studies of iconic figures, comparing old and new industry models, and synthesizing that history into a personal approach. This is entirely desk-based analytical and writing work: historical research, case-study synthesis, and comparative argument construction, tasks squarely inside what task-exposure research associates with high automation exposure. Current AI systems can already research historical case studies and draft comparative analyses competently, though recent capability benchmarks on real occupational deliverables still show AI falling short of full parity with human experts on integrative, judgment-heavy writing. At 24 months, realized adoption for this kind of synthesis work is real but partial, and no general-studies designation or foundational-prerequisite role protects the course from that exposure.

By 2031, AI research and writing tools will plausibly handle much of the historical case-study synthesis and comparative-analysis work this course assigns, consistent with the trend of rapidly lengthening AI task-time horizons and with observed usage already concentrated in computer-mediated writing and research tasks. Verification burden is moderate, not protective: a flawed AI-drafted comparison of A&R eras is a correctable academic-writing error rather than a high-stakes failure, so expert review is valuable but not a strict gate on deployment. The course does feed into Managing an Established Act as a prerequisite, giving it a modest downstream role, but that alone does not meet the bar for a foundational-scaffolding cap. With no institutional lock-in otherwise, the rating rises to High as the writing and synthesis tasks become increasingly deployable.

A decade out, under considerable uncertainty, AI systems are plausibly capable of producing sophisticated historical and comparative analysis of the music-industry deal-making this course covers, substantially eroding the rationale for students to personally generate every case-study synthesis. Real-deliverable capability benchmarks show frontier models already approaching, though not yet matching, human-expert performance on integrative professional writing, and that gap is likely to narrow further by 2036, even as adoption historically lags raw capability. Without a general-studies designation or a strong foundational role — its only downstream link is a single prerequisite relationship to one later course — nothing structurally caps the rating. The central case holds at High, with genuine uncertainty about whether the course's personal-synthesis rationale is replaced or merely supplemented by AI-assisted historical research.
MUS 3880.d: Building directly on MUS 1892: Artist Discovery and Development, the students in the course examine more advanced concepts and practices in artists and repertoire. While digging deeper into the history of artists and repertoire and record labels, students focus more acutely on the backroom negotiations and deal making that has contributed to success or failure by examining various case studies of iconic figures in this field. Students examine and compare both old and new models of artists and repertoire practice. Ultimately, students gain an understanding of how industry professionals have navigated the complex politics between the various stakeholders in the music industry. Students construct their own personal approach to artists and repertoire by synthesizing various historical methods and techniques in this field.

r: Music Industry Contract Negotiation combines drafting and marking up deals with a large portion of the semester spent practicing negotiation skill through live role-playing exercises that integrate theory and psychology, aiming to balance artists' aspirations, personal goals, and legal obligations. Contract drafting and markup are exposed to current AI drafting tools, but the course's dominant activity is live, real-time interpersonal negotiation practice, a task-exposure category the research associates with lower automation exposure than writing or coding work. Verification burden is high because a negotiated deal that mishandles legal obligations or an artist's interests carries real cost, so expert human judgment stays central to checking any AI-assisted draft language. At 24 months, the embodied negotiation-practice core and the legal stakes involved keep realized automatability limited despite genuine erosion of the pure drafting-task component.

By 2031, AI contract-drafting and negotiation-simulation tools will plausibly be more capable and more commonly used to generate first-draft deal language and even role-play counterpart positions, but the course's core instrumental task — a student personally practicing live negotiation under real-time pressure with faculty feedback — remains an embodied, interpersonal skill that such tools do not replace. High verification burden persists: the jagged-frontier finding that AI users misjudge accuracy outside a model's true competence is directly relevant to unsupervised reliance on AI-drafted contract terms in a domain with real legal and financial consequences. With no general-studies designation and no foundational role protecting the course, the rating still holds Low on the strength of the dampening effect from verification burden and embodied negotiation practice, even as the surrounding drafting tasks grow more automatable.

Ten years out, under wide uncertainty, AI negotiation-simulation and contract-drafting tools are plausibly sophisticated enough to handle a meaningful share of deal-structuring work and to serve as realistic practice partners, which would erode some of the course's rationale even for the live-practice component. The countervailing factor is that the verification burden around legally binding, financially consequential negotiated agreements remains protective in principle, since errors are costly and non-obvious to catch without expert review, consistent with the jagged-frontier evidence on miscalibrated trust in high-stakes domains. With no institutional lock-in or foundational-prerequisite role to cap the rating further, the central case moves to Medium: real erosion in the drafting and simulated-practice components, tempered by the persistent need for human judgment in consequential deal-making and by uncertainty about how far AI negotiation tools actually diffuse into legal practice.
MUS 3882.d: This course focuses on developing the skills necessary to initiate and broker various types of contracts and/or deals related to the contemporary music industry. While integrating theory and psychology into the class, students spend a large portion of the semester practicing their negotiation skills in live role-playing exercises. Through such activities, students gain the ability to draft deals/contracts with authority and complete mark-ups and final versions that balance artists' aspirations, personal goals, and legal obligations.

r: Managing an Established Act is a capstone-style course, drawing on the program's prior artist-management sequence, where students learn to sustain a career over time: navigating market trends, maintaining and growing an audience through marketing strategies, re-branding acts for new markets, and analyzing case studies of career management and revival. This is desk-based strategic and analytical work — market analysis, marketing-plan drafting, case-study synthesis — falling within the Computer & Mathematical category that observed-usage data identifies as AI's largest current-use share. Current AI tools already generate competent marketing strategy drafts and case-study comparisons, though firm-level AI adoption remains well under half of US businesses, so realized deployment of these tools in actual artist-management practice is still uneven at 24 months. No general-studies designation or foundational-prerequisite role protects this terminal, high-prerequisite capstone course from that exposure.

By 2031, AI-generated marketing strategy, audience-trend analysis, and re-branding case studies will plausibly be standard inputs to artist-management work, consistent with the trend of rapidly lengthening AI task-time horizons in complex, multi-step business-strategy tasks. Diffusion research shows firm-level AI adoption lagging raw capability, but a specialized, digitally native field like music-industry management is a plausible early adopter given how concentrated current AI usage already is in computer-mediated analytical work. Verification burden is moderate, not protective, since a flawed AI-drafted marketing strategy is a correctable business judgment rather than a high-stakes, hard-to-catch error. With no institutional lock-in and the course sitting at the terminal end of its sequence rather than a foundational one, the rating rises to High as the strategic-analysis tasks become increasingly ones AI can competently draft.

A decade out, under considerable uncertainty about both capability and diffusion, AI systems are plausibly deeply integrated into artist-management workflows, generating market analysis, marketing strategy, and re-branding plans that once required a manager's own synthesis of case studies and trend data. Macro-level productivity effects from AI diffusion have historically been modest even as capability accelerates, so some caution is warranted about assuming full automation of strategic judgment in a relationship-driven field like artist management. Still, with no general-studies designation, no accreditation mandate, and no foundational role in the curriculum to cap the rating, the central case holds at High: the course's core analytical and strategic-writing tasks are squarely within AI's growing competence, even as the human relationship-management and creative-vision aspects of the role remain the most durable, least certain residue.
MUS 3884.d: This course focuses on how to sustain an artist's career over the long term. Students learn to navigate through changes in market trends to ensure that their artists remain relevant in a dynamic environment. The course covers maintaining existing audiences while attracting new ones through numerous marketing strategies. Students learn to re-brand and re-launch existing acts for new times, markets, and audiences. The course examines a range of case studies, regarding how to manage and elevate an existing act as well as re- imagine the career of an iconic artist who has fallen out of favor.

r: Artist Deal Suite trains students to identify and analyze contemporary music industry deal terms—licensing, recording, publishing, and touring contracts—so they can communicate competently with lawyers, executives, and other stakeholders. Contract review and clause-by-clause interpretation are squarely within current AI strengths: models summarize, flag, and compare legal boilerplate reliably at the sentence level. Observed-usage data already shows document analysis and legal-adjacent writing as prominent AI use cases among knowledge workers, and adoption is spreading into small-business and educational contexts. Still, the jagged-frontier finding means AI reasoning about contract terms outside well-trodden clause patterns invites overconfident, uncalibrated answers, so a human who understands deal structure remains necessary to catch consequential misreads. No general-studies or licensure mandate applies. At 24 months the instrumental need is only partially eroded, landing Medium.

By 2031, contract-analysis tools will be materially more capable and far more broadly deployed across the music business, consistent with the rapid task-time-horizon growth documented in recent capability trend research. Students entering the field will increasingly rely on AI to draft first-pass summaries of licensing, recording, and touring agreements, shifting the course's instrumental center from performing the analysis toward directing and checking it. Verification burden softens as models specialize on contract language, though genuinely novel or adversarial deal terms will still reward a human who understands the underlying legal logic. No general-studies or accreditation lock constrains this business elective, so nothing structurally protects the course from this drift. The balance of realized automation and thinning verification need pushes the rating to High, while negotiation-communication skills the course also builds retain independent value.

A decade out, under a wide-uncertainty central case, AI systems will handle routine music-industry contract analysis with little oversight, and adoption will have diffused well beyond early-adopter firms even if aggregate productivity effects remain modest by macroeconomic measures. The specific instrumental task this course teaches—reading and interpreting deal terms—will largely be something students direct AI to do rather than perform from scratch. Harder to displace is the course's secondary function: preparing students to communicate credibly with lawyers and executives, an interpersonal, judgment-based skill that resists full automation even as the analytical substrate is automated. Given no institutional lock and no foundational role for later coursework, the rating holds High, with real but bounded uncertainty about how much hands-on contract literacy programs will still require by 2036.
MUS 3885.d: This course introduces students to a variety of contemporary music industry deals and contract types. Students identify and analyze the conventional terms and conditions within these various documents. A range of legal terms and procedures are discussed with the goal of improving students' ability to communicate with lawyers, record executives, and other major stakeholders in the music industry.

r: Live Tour Management teaches students to plan and budget tours across venue scales, developing logistics organization, time management, and financial forecasting for local, national, and international outings. These are largely digital planning tasks—spreadsheet-based budgeting, scheduling, routing—that current AI tools already assist with credibly, and observed-usage data places planning and organizing work among prominent categories of AI use. Realized deployment specifically inside touring logistics remains uneven; diffusion research shows only a minority of firms have operationalized AI tools even where capability exists, and small independent tour operations lag further behind. Verification burden is moderate: a forecasting or scheduling error has real financial consequences, so judgment about vendor relationships, contingencies, and venue-specific quirks still needs a trained planner. No general-studies or accreditation mandate applies. At 24 months the instrumental case is only partly eroded, landing Medium.

By 2031, budgeting, routing, and scheduling software embedded with AI assistance will likely be standard in the touring business, and capability-trend research suggests forecasting and logistics-optimization tasks—well-structured, data-rich problems—sit inside AI's strengthening frontier. Students will increasingly direct AI tools to generate draft budgets and routing plans rather than build them from first principles, shifting the course's center of gravity toward reviewing, adjusting, and defending AI output to venues and artists. Verification burden eases somewhat as tools mature, though local contingencies—weather, permitting, venue idiosyncrasies—still reward human judgment. No institutional lock constrains this elective, and it does not underpin later required coursework. Given the well-defined, quantifiable nature of the planning tasks involved, the rating rises to High, while acknowledging real uncertainty about how quickly small touring operations actually adopt these tools.

A decade out, under a central-case reading of continuing capability growth, most of the quantifiable planning work this course teaches—budgeting, scheduling, logistics routing—should be substantially automatable and, per adoption trends, increasingly deployed even in mid-size touring operations, though macro-level productivity studies suggest diffusion still lags capability meaningfully. What likely persists is the negotiation and relationship layer: dealing with promoters, crews, and unpredictable on-the-ground circumstances that resist full digitization. Because the course carries no general-studies or accreditation lock and does not scaffold later required courses, nothing structurally protects it from this erosion. The rating holds High, with the caveat that ten-year forecasts for a fast-moving, tool-dependent commercial practice carry substantial uncertainty about exactly which planning tasks remain human-directed versus fully delegated to AI systems.
MUS 3886.d: This course examines the details of designing and managing a live tour at a local, national, and international scale. In the current music industry, live touring is often times the most important and lucrative component of an artist's career. Students learn how to logistically plan and budget for various sizes of venues and lengths of outings. Students hone their skills particularly in logistics organization, time management, and financial forecasting.

r: This course moves students from a finished arrangement through pre-production, recording, mixing, mastering, and release, with hands-on studio time working alongside professional producers and engineers. The instrumental core is embodied and collaborative: operating physical recording equipment, making real-time judgment calls in the room, and navigating what the course itself calls the politics of the recording studio. Current AI mixing and mastering plugins handle isolated technical steps competently, but the course's actual task—guiding a full production from song selection through final master while working with people—is not something students currently offload to AI wholesale. Verification burden is real: production quality judgments require a trained ear that catches subtle errors AI tools miss. No general-studies mandate applies, but the embodied, interpersonal, studio-based nature of the work keeps the 24-month instrumental need largely intact. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI mixing and mastering tools will be considerably more capable and likely embedded directly into standard studio software, consistent with the fast task-time-horizon growth documented in recent capability research. Even so, the course's defining tasks—collaborating with a producer and engineer in a physical studio, making real-time creative and technical decisions, and navigating interpersonal studio dynamics—remain resistant to substitution because they are embodied and relationally grounded rather than purely computational. Verification burden stays meaningful: judging whether an AI-assisted mix serves the song still requires trained listening. The dampening effect of low embodiment and low verification-burden protection outweighs the rising technical capability at this horizon. No institutional lock applies, but the hands-on studio requirement functions as a practical anchor. The rating remains Low, though the technical portion of the workflow is visibly eroding faster than the interpersonal core.

Under a wide-uncertainty ten-year central case, AI audio production tools should handle the bulk of routine mixing, mastering, and even arrangement-level decisions with high fidelity, and diffusion into commercial and educational studios should be substantially further along than today. At that point the technical substrate of record production is plausibly automatable enough that the course's realized task-exposure crosses into higher territory, even though the embodied studio-collaboration experience the course also emphasizes resists full replacement. This is the most speculative horizon in the set: it assumes both continued rapid capability growth and meaningful diffusion into music-education settings, neither guaranteed. With no general-studies or accreditation lock and no foundational role for later required courses, nothing structurally holds the rating down at this horizon, and it rises to High, held with real uncertainty.
MUS 3888.d: This class focuses on the processes of moving from a finished arrangement in the rehearsal room to a master recording. Students learn about selecting the appropriate songs, quality control, pre-production, choosing and working with a producer and engineer, goal setting, mixing, mastering, and the politics of the recording studio. Throughout the semester, students analyze and discuss the production of iconic songs and albums, exploring its effects on the entire songwriting and creative process. Partnering with local studios, students have an opportunity to gain hands-on experience in a recording studio, working with industry producers and engineers to perform, conduct, mix, and master their own compositions.

r: This seminar asks students to critically analyze how popular music has voiced political and social concerns across U.S. and international contexts, engaging theoretical frameworks through discussion and written analysis. Task-exposure research draws a distinction relevant here: critical-thinking skills are strongly negatively associated with AI exposure, while writing skills are strongly positively associated—and this course sits at the intersection, pairing seminar-style critical discourse with written analytical output. Current models can already draft competent essays on music-and-politics themes, which erodes the instrumental need to produce the written artifact from scratch, but the live, seminar-based critical exchange the course centers is harder to substitute. No general-studies designation locks this elective into the transfer core. On balance, at 24 months the writing-adjacent tasks are meaningfully exposed while the discussion-based critical-thinking core is not, yielding Medium.

By 2031, AI-generated analytical writing on music and political movements will be fluent and widely accessible, consistent with productivity research showing professional writing tasks completed faster and rated higher quality with AI assistance. The instrumental rationale for students to produce written socio-political analysis unaided weakens substantially, and with no general-studies or accreditation mandate to hold the course in a protected core, that erosion is not capped. The seminar-discussion component retains real-time interpersonal value, but as graded deliverables shift toward writing that AI can competently draft, the balance tips further. Verification burden is modest for this kind of humanities analysis—incorrect interpretive claims are not high-stakes the way clinical or legal errors are—so little protection comes from that factor either. The rating rises to High, acknowledging genuine uncertainty about how such seminars are restructured under ubiquitous AI writing tools.

A decade out, under a central-case view of continued capability growth, AI should be capable of generating sophisticated, well-sourced critical analysis connecting popular music to political movements, and such tools will likely be a default part of how students draft coursework across humanities disciplines. The seminar's discussion format offers some ongoing rationale, but as an instrumental matter—performing the interpretive and written work the course is built around—AI increasingly does this competently. With no general-studies lock, no accreditation floor, and no downstream required courses depending on this one, nothing structurally protects the rating from remaining elevated. The honest hedge is that ten years is long enough for pedagogy itself to shift toward AI-integrated critical-thinking exercises this framework cannot fully anticipate, but on the current task description, the rating holds High.
MUS 3890.d: Taking an interdisciplinary approach, this course examines how popular music has voiced the concerns of the masses and the marginalized to bring about social awareness and change. This seminar-style course challenges students to critically think about, and listen to, a variety of politically driven music from the U.S. and abroad. Discussions of theoretical frameworks for analyzing politics and popular music, exploring definitions and basic concepts are deployed throughout the semester. Students explore music's role in the major socio-political movements in American history as well as several cases outside of the US context. Students gain a greater appreciation for the ability of popular music to shape the social and political world.

r: Detroit Music Heritage surveys the city's musical development—from Motown to techno—through interdisciplinary readings, listening, and film drawn from history, sociology, ethnomusicology, anthropology, and journalism, producing student analysis and writing about music's role in urban social history. This is fundamentally a research-and-writing survey course, and task-exposure research classifies writing tasks as strongly positively associated with AI exposure; models can already synthesize historical and cultural material into competent survey-style prose. The interdisciplinary breadth adds some resistance, since integrating disparate source types well still benefits from human synthesis, but the core deliverables—reading responses, analytical essays—are squarely within current AI capability. No general-studies designation locks this course into a protected transfer core. At 24 months the instrumental need for students to independently produce this analysis is already meaningfully eroded, though not yet fully so, landing Medium.

By 2031, AI systems will handle interdisciplinary historical synthesis—combining musicological, sociological, and journalistic sources into coherent narrative analysis—with substantially greater fluency, and observed-usage patterns already show research-and-writing tasks among the most common AI applications in educational and knowledge-work settings. The course's central instrumental activity, producing written cultural-historical analysis, becomes something AI can draft competently, shifting the pedagogical value toward evaluating, correcting, and extending AI-generated work rather than generating it unaided. Verification burden remains low-to-moderate for this kind of humanities interpretation, since factual or interpretive errors carry modest real-world cost, offering little protective dampening. With no general-studies or accreditation lock holding the course in place, the erosion is not capped. The rating rises to High, with appropriate caution about how quickly cultural-history survey pedagogy actually adapts its assignments in response.

Under a wide-uncertainty ten-year central case, AI should be capable of producing rich, well-integrated interdisciplinary cultural history on demand, and such capability will likely have diffused well into educational contexts even though macro-level adoption research suggests aggregate productivity effects remain gradual. The specific instrumental tasks this course builds—synthesizing readings and producing analytical writing about music's social role—are plausibly among the more thoroughly automated in the humanities survey category by this horizon. No general-studies designation, accreditation floor, or downstream-course dependency protects the rating from this trajectory. The genuine hedge is that ten years also allows time for the course's assessment design to shift toward oral, project-based, or AI-collaborative formats that would change this calculus, a possibility this framework cannot resolve. On the described task profile as it stands, the rating holds High.
MUS 3891.d: In this course, students explore the crucial role that music has played in Detroit's development, and, conversely, how the city's unique identity encouraged its particular sonic trajectory. From Motown to techno, Detroit is widely known as an important site of American musical development. Countering narratives of Detroit as a "dying" bankrupt city in perpetual decline, this course shows its vitality and tenacity through a social history of the city's rich musical heritage. Incorporating an interdisciplinary approach, this course explores a diversity of readings, listening, and films from a range of academic fields including: history, sociology, ethnomusicology, anthropology, and journalism.

r: Live Sound trains students to run front-of-house and monitor mixes in real time across varied stage contexts, working hands-on with professional PA systems, mixers, and microphones. The instrumental core is embodied, real-time psychomotor and perceptual work—listening critically in a live acoustic space and adjusting a physical mixing console under performance conditions—an activity task-exposure research does not classify as automatable; manual, physically situated work with real-time feedback loops sits well outside AI's current operational range. Verification burden is also high: a mixing error during a live show is immediately audible and effectively unrecoverable, so a trained engineer's judgment is not optional. No general-studies designation applies, and no licensure gates the course, but the embodiment and verification factors alone keep the rating anchored. At 24 months there is no meaningful erosion of the instrumental need; rating Low.

AI audio tools will keep improving through 2031, and automated live-mixing assistance may enter some professional PA systems, but the course's actual instrumental task—a student physically operating a console, reading a room's acoustics in real time, and responding to unpredictable live performance conditions—remains embodied in a way that resists substitution. Verification burden stays high because live-sound mistakes are immediate and public, and jagged-frontier research on miscalibrated AI trust in unfamiliar conditions is particularly relevant to a domain defined by every-venue variability. Diffusion research indicates AI adoption is still uneven across firms generally, and live-event audio is a niche, equipment-heavy context likely to lag further. Neither general-studies nor accreditation factors apply, but embodiment and verification burden jointly hold the rating down across this horizon. The rating remains Low, with modest confidence given the pace of audio-tool development.

A decade out, under a wide-uncertainty central case, AI-assisted live-sound tools may handle more of the routine gain-staging and EQ groundwork, but the defining instrumental competence this course builds—real-time, embodied judgment about how a mix sounds and feels in a live room, adjusted continuously during a performance—remains a fundamentally in-person, psychomotor skill that automation does not perform on the student's behalf. The verification-burden argument strengthens rather than weakens at scale: live audio failures are public and immediate regardless of how sophisticated the underlying tools become. No institutional lock protects the course, but none is needed given how strongly embodiment and verification burden anchor it. The honest hedge is that automation could reshape supporting production tasks around live sound considerably by 2036, but the rating for this specific applied-skill course holds Low.
MUS 3892.d: This course covers the fundamentals of running live sound in various stage contexts for a range of instrumentations and musical styles. Students learn how to produce front of house ("FOH") sound mixes and onstage monitor mixes. Working with professional PA systems, mixers, microphones, and other musical equipment, students have ample opportunity to gain practical hands-on experience in this subject.

r: This course examines cultural conflict within core elements of Hip-Hop culture and its effects on gender and social identity, asking students to think critically about Hip-Hop through interdisciplinary engagement with literature, film, and music. Task-exposure research separates critical thinking, negatively associated with AI exposure, from writing, strongly positively associated; this course's graded deliverables likely lean toward written cultural analysis and discussion responses, placing much of the realized work within AI's current competence even as the underlying critical-thinking goal resists full substitution. Current models draft passable cultural-criticism essays on hip-hop themes already. No general-studies designation locks this course into a protected transfer core, so no institutional constraint offsets the exposure. At 24 months the instrumental need for unaided written analysis is meaningfully eroded while the seminar's discursive and interpretive goals remain intact, yielding Medium.

By 2031, AI-generated cultural criticism and interdisciplinary analysis connecting music, literature, and film will be fluent and broadly accessible, consistent with evidence that professional writing tasks see substantial time savings and quality gains with AI assistance. As with comparable humanities-writing courses, this pushes the instrumental balance further toward AI performing the analytical-writing deliverables the course is built around, while discussion-based engagement offers a partial but incomplete counterweight. Verification burden is modest for this kind of interpretive cultural analysis, since incorrect claims carry low real-world cost, so little protection comes from that factor. With no general-studies or accreditation lock in place, nothing caps the erosion at this horizon. The rating rises to High, while acknowledging that how instructors redesign assessments in response to AI writing tools will materially affect the real trajectory.

A decade out, under a central-case reading of continued capability growth and diffusion into educational settings, AI should be capable of producing sophisticated interdisciplinary cultural criticism connecting hip-hop, literature, film, and social identity with minimal expert correction needed. The course's discussion-based, critically engaged format offers some ongoing pedagogical rationale, but as an instrumental matter the written and analytical work AI performs competently. No general-studies designation, accreditation floor, or downstream required course depends on this one, so nothing structurally protects the rating from remaining elevated. The genuine uncertainty is whether humanities pedagogy shifts substantially toward oral, project-based, or AI-collaborative assessment in ways that would change the underlying task profile—a real possibility this ten-year horizon cannot rule out. On the described task profile, the rating holds High.
MUS 3895.d: This course seeks to examine the long-standing cultural warfare that exists among core elements of Hip-Hop culture and the impact such challenges have on gender and social identities. Students will think critically about Hip-Hop music beyond the scope of entertainment through the examination of literature, films, and music that provide interdisciplinary discourse on Hip-Hop in our society.

r: This applied course develops advanced technical facility and improvisational ability on a student's chosen instrument through progressively challenging exercises across musical genres, building directly on prior intermediate coursework. The instrumental core is embodied psychomotor skill—physically executing technique on an instrument in real time and developing a personal creative approach to improvisation—an activity task-exposure research does not treat as automatable; generative music AI can produce improvised-sounding audio, but it does not substitute for a student's own developing physical and creative capacity. Verification burden is real: a teacher's ear is needed to assess technical progress and interpretive choices in real time. No general-studies designation applies, and while the course sits within a sequential technique track feeding a follow-on course, that scaffolding role is secondary to embodiment here. At 24 months there is no meaningful erosion; rating Low.

AI music-generation tools will be considerably more capable and more widely used across the commercial music landscape by 2031, but that reshapes the market for recorded and composed music, which is explicitly outside this rating's scope. The instrumental question is whether a student still needs to develop advanced physical technique and improvisational facility on their own instrument, and nothing about generative AI substitutes for that developmental process; embodiment and the associated verification burden—an instructor assessing live technical execution—both remain fully intact across a single catalog cycle. Diffusion research indicates AI adoption is uneven even where capability exists, and applied instrumental pedagogy is far from the kinds of white-collar knowledge work where adoption concentrates. No institutional lock is needed given how strongly embodiment anchors the course. The rating remains Low.

Under a wide-uncertainty ten-year central case, synthetic and AI-assisted music production will likely be pervasive in the broader music economy, but the specific competence Advanced Techniques and Improvisation I builds—a student's own physical technique and improvisational judgment on their instrument—is not a task AI performs on the learner's behalf regardless of how convincing generative audio becomes. Embodiment is the defining feature of the coursework, and that does not erode with model capability the way a purely digital analytical task would. The honest caveat is that the surrounding professional and commercial context for improvising musicians may be considerably more AI-exposed than the instrumental necessity of the applied-study course itself, and how programs structure improvisation training could shift in ways this framework cannot fully anticipate. The rating holds Low.
MUS 3910.d: Building on Intermediate Techniques and Improv I and II, this course provides students the opportunity to develop advanced technical facility and improvisational abilities on their chosen instrument. This involves a logical progression of advanced-level exercises and applications. Students are challenged to experiment with advanced level techniques to further develop a creative approach to improvisation. The class situates technical vocabulary and improvisational skills within a variety of challenging musical contexts across numerous genres.

r: This course continues the technique-and-improvisation sequence, deepening a student's facility on their chosen instrument through further progressive exercises and application across genres, building directly on the prior semester's coursework in the same instrument area. As with its prerequisite, the instrumental core is embodied psychomotor and creative skill—physically executing advanced technique and developing improvisational judgment in real time—which task-exposure research does not classify as automatable in any meaningful sense. Verification requires an instructor's trained ear assessing live performance and interpretive choices, not a text or audio artifact that AI could evaluate or generate on the student's behalf. No general-studies designation applies to this upper-division applied course, and while it caps a two-course technique sequence, that scaffolding factor is not the binding constraint here—embodiment is. At 24 months the instrumental need is fully intact; rating Low.

By 2031, generative music AI will be markedly more capable and will reshape parts of the commercial music economy—composition, backing tracks, production—but that is a market and enrollment consideration explicitly outside this rating's instrumental question. Whether a student still needs to develop advanced physical technique and improvisational facility through hands-on practice is unchanged: no model performs the psychomotor and creative developmental act the course builds, and the associated verification—live instructor assessment—still requires the trained human. Diffusion research shows AI adoption remains uneven and concentrated in knowledge-work settings quite unlike applied instrumental pedagogy. Across a single catalog cycle the applied-study requirement holds fully. The instrumental case remains Low; the broader improvisation-adjacent commercial landscape may shift considerably beneath it, but the course's task rationale does not change.

A decade out, under a wide-uncertainty central case, synthetic and AI-assisted music generation will likely be highly capable and pervasive, yet live human improvisation—the specific competence this course develops—is not a task AI executes on a performer's behalf; embodiment is the entire point of the coursework. The most plausible ten-year change is in what improvising musicians are paid to do professionally and how AI tools enter individual practice routines, not in whether learning to improvise on one's instrument requires actually doing it. The rating stays Low, with the honest caveat that the surrounding labor market for improvising performers is considerably more exposed to AI substitution than the instrumental necessity of this applied-study course itself, a distinction this framework holds firmly throughout this horizon.
MUS 3920.d: This course builds directly on the previous semester's iteration, providing students an opportunity to further develop a deeper facility on their chosen instrument. This development involves a logical progression of exercises and application. Students continue to experiment with advanced level techniques to further develop a creative approach to improvisation. The course situates technical vocabulary and improvisational skills within a variety of musical contexts across numerous genres.

r: Group Performance Instruction III continues group instrument instruction begun in the prior course in this sequence, developing applied performance skill in a group instructional setting on a specific instrument. The instrumental core is embodied, real-time musical performance and ensemble coordination—physically playing an instrument alongside peers under an instructor's live guidance—an activity task-exposure research places outside AI's automatable range; manual, in-person, psychomotor skill development does not transfer to a model regardless of how convincing generative audio synthesis becomes. Verification burden is high in the sense that matters here: an instructor must hear and correct technique live, in real time, something no digital artifact substitutes for. No general-studies designation applies to this applied course. At 24 months there is no erosion of the instrumental need; the competence is intrinsically embodied and group-based. Rating Low.

AI music tools will grow substantially more capable by 2031 and will affect parts of the recorded and composed music economy, but that market shift is explicitly outside this instrumental rating. The question for a group performance course is whether students still need hands-on, in-person instruction to develop applied playing skill together, and the answer is unchanged: no AI system substitutes for the physical, ensemble-coordinated practice of playing an instrument under live group instruction. Verification and embodiment both keep the human instructional relationship necessary across a single catalog cycle. Diffusion research indicates AI adoption concentrates in digital knowledge work, a poor match for embodied group instrumental pedagogy. No general-studies or accreditation lock is needed given how firmly embodiment anchors this course. The rating remains Low across this horizon.

Under a wide-uncertainty ten-year central case, AI-generated and AI-assisted music will likely be pervasive and highly convincing, but group performance instruction develops a specific, non-substitutable competence: students physically playing together, coordinating in real time, under live instructor correction. That is not a task AI executes on the students' behalf regardless of how far generative audio capability advances by 2036. The more plausible long-run change is in the broader professional context these students eventually enter, not in whether learning to play an instrument in an ensemble setting requires embodied practice. No institutional lock applies, and none is needed given the strength of the embodiment and verification factors. The rating holds Low, with the standard caveat that surrounding commercial music markets are far more AI-exposed than this applied-instruction course's instrumental core.
MUS 3940.d: This is a continuation of MUS 2950: Group Performance II, offering group instruction on a specific instrument.

r: Group Performance Instruction IV continues small-group applied study on a specific instrument, building tone, technique, ensemble listening, and live musicianship under direct coaching, following directly from MUS 3940. The work is embodied performance and real-time coached feedback, not the production of a finished musical artifact a model could substitute. Task-exposure research classifies manual, in-person, psychomotor activity as low-exposure even as it finds writing and symbolic tasks positively associated with exposure. Generative audio tools can render instrumental sound, but that capability does not replace a student's own developing technique judged live by an instructor's ear. Verification here strictly requires a musician-instructor present in the room; no AI output substitutes for that judgment. NASM-aligned applied-study norms and the sequential group-instruction structure reinforce this as accumulated embodied training. At 24 months the instrumental need for this course shows no erosion.

By 2031, AI music-generation tools will be considerably more capable and may reshape parts of the commercial music economy, but that is a market question the rating explicitly excludes. Group Performance Instruction IV asks whether a student still needs to build live technique on an instrument in a coached group setting, and nothing in AI's trajectory substitutes for that psychomotor development. Embodiment and verification both stay protective: the skill is defined by real-time execution and judged by a present instructor's ear, not by an evaluable digital artifact. The jagged-frontier finding that AI users perform worse outside a model's competence zone, paired with mis-calibrated trust, underscores why live coached listening cannot be replaced by automated feedback for a developing performer. Across one catalog cycle the applied-study requirement is essentially unchanged, and the rating remains Low, anchored by embodiment rather than by any institutional lock.

Under a wide-uncertainty ten-year horizon, synthetic and AI-assisted music production will likely be pervasive, and capability-trend evidence on rapidly lengthening task horizons suggests continued fast progress in generative audio specifically. Even so, the competence this course builds — a student's own instrumental technique, ensemble listening, and tone production developed under live coaching — is not a task AI performs on the learner's behalf; the embodied act of performing is the point, not an artifact that could be generated instead. The more plausible ten-year shift is in the surrounding music economy and in how coached practice incorporates AI tools for reference or accompaniment, not in whether a student must still develop live instrumental skill. The rating holds Low, with the acknowledged caveat that predictions about generative-audio capability at ten years carry real uncertainty even though the applied-study rationale itself does not depend on that capability.
MUS 3950.d: This is a continuation of MUS 3940L Group Performance III, offering group instruction on a specific instrument.

r: Internship in Music places a student in a supervised professional placement — arranged through the Classroom to Career Hub and overseen by a music faculty member — where requirements vary by placement and may span performance support, arts administration, teaching assistance, or production work. Because the tasks are placement-dependent and site-supervised, the instrumental value lies in guided, real-world professional experience rather than in a single automatable deliverable. Diffusion data show only a minority of US firms had adopted AI in workplace processes by late 2025, so most placement environments still run on largely human-supervised workflows. Faculty and site-supervisor verification of a student's professional conduct and judgment is central to the course design and cannot be delegated to a model. At 24 months, the supervised placement structure keeps the instrumental need essentially intact.

By 2031, AI tools will likely be embedded in many of the administrative, research, and communication tasks an internship placement might involve, and observed-usage data already shows writing and office-style tasks are prominent among current AI use. That said, the course's instrumental core is supervised professional practice and faculty-guided reflection on a real placement, not a specific work product AI could generate in the student's stead. Because placements vary widely and faculty oversight of professional judgment remains built into the course, verification stays anchored in direct supervision rather than in checking an AI-produced deliverable. Diffusion of AI into music-related workplaces will likely be uneven across the placement types this course draws on. The rating holds Low, reflecting the supervised, experiential design rather than the automatability of any one task a placement might include.

At ten years the uncertainty is substantial: which professional tasks an internship placement emphasizes could shift considerably as AI reshapes administrative and creative-support work across the music industry, and macro estimates suggest such diffusion happens unevenly and gradually even under optimistic capability assumptions. Still, the course's defining feature — a supervised, faculty-mediated placement building professional judgment and workplace competence under direct oversight — is structurally resistant to substitution because its value is the guided experience itself, not a deliverable. Even if AI increasingly assists with the tasks a student performs on-site, the requirement to complete supervised placement hours and receive faculty evaluation would persist. The rating remains Low, with the honest caveat that the content of available placements a decade out may look quite different even as the instrumental need for supervised experiential learning is unlikely to disappear.
MUS 3980.d: Supervised by a faculty member in the Department of Music, internships provide practical, hands-on experience in a professional field related to the major. Internship placements must be established prior to enrollment in this course in consultation with the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub. Internship requirements vary by department.
