r: Musics of Latin America is a lecture-and-writing survey examining how colonialism, race, urbanization, and diaspora inform genres from folkloric to contemporary popular and electronic music. The work is analytical and written — interpreting cultural and historical context and applying critical frameworks to musical examples — tasks that task-exposure research associates positively with AI exposure given their textual, non-manual character. The course carries a General Studies Arts and Humanities and Global Diversity designation, a gtPathways-aligned transfer-core mandate that keeps it institutionally required regardless of task-level erosion. At 24 months, AI can already draft competent cultural-historical commentary on named genres, but the general-education requirement anchors the course in the curriculum independent of that capability. The rating is Low, driven primarily by the institutional lock rather than by any inherent resistance of the writing-and-analysis tasks themselves.

By 2031, AI models will likely produce fluent, well-sourced writing on colonialism, diaspora, and genre history in Latin American music, substantially eroding the rationale that students must personally generate this analytical prose. Observed-usage data already shows writing and research-adjacent tasks are prominent in current AI use, and that trend is expected to deepen. The instrumental case shifts toward the student's own critical judgment, contextual synthesis, and ability to evaluate AI-generated cultural analysis rather than reproduce it from scratch. Because the course carries a General Studies Arts and Humanities and Global Diversity designation, the gtPathways transfer mandate caps the rating at Medium: erosion of the writing task is real, but the general-education requirement keeps the course necessary across a catalog cycle regardless. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting rising task-level automatability capped by institutional lock-in.

A decade out, AI-generated cultural and historical commentary on global musics will likely be sophisticated and widely available, and the rationale for students to independently produce comparable written analysis is substantially weakened in the central case. Even so, the General Studies Arts and Humanities and Global Diversity designation persists as a gtPathways transfer-core requirement that is unlikely to be dropped merely because AI can write about the material, since the mandate reflects institutional and transfer-credit structure rather than task difficulty. The rating holds Medium, capped from rising further by that designation even as the underlying analytical tasks become highly automatable. The genuine uncertainty concerns how such survey courses are taught and assessed under ubiquitous generative writing tools, not whether the gtPathways requirement itself persists across the ten-year horizon.
MUS 4000.d: This course explores the diverse, vibrant musical traditions of Latin America. Particular attention will be given to the many ways in which cultural, historical and political developments throughout the Western hemisphere both inform and are informed by musical practices. Students will become familiar with some of the most influential and popular Latin musics and musicians, as well as the larger cultural context from which they emerge and continue to operate. Histories and theories of colonialism, race, urbanization/modernization, and diaspora will be applied as a means of understanding various functions and meanings the music has come to articulate. Genres to be studied range from traditional, folkloric, and religious music to contemporary popular, electronic, and film music.

r: Senior Seminar in Music is a one-credit capstone built almost entirely around in-class, real-time peer interaction: students give and receive peer-review feedback, discuss what it means to be an educated musician, examine sub-disciplines, and plan post-graduation steps with visiting specialists. The instrumental content is the live discussion and mentoring exchange, not a document a model could generate. Task-exposure research finds real-time interpersonal exchange far less exposed than solitary writing or research tasks, and that distinction applies directly here since the course explicitly confines its work to class time. AI could help a student draft career materials outside class, but that is peripheral to the seminar's actual instrumental content, which is peer dialogue and specialist mentorship delivered in person. At 24 months the rating is Low, anchored by the real-time interpersonal design of the course.

By 2031, AI career-advising tools will likely be common for drafting resumes, researching sub-disciplines, or outlining post-graduation plans, and some students may lean on them heavily for such preparatory work. But Senior Seminar in Music is structured so its instrumental core happens inside class time as live peer-review and discussion, not as an external deliverable students produce and submit; the course description is explicit that the work is largely contained to class sessions. Real-time interpersonal exchange between graduating peers and visiting specialists remains a form of engagement task-exposure research continues to treat as comparatively resistant, even as adjacent preparatory tasks become AI-assisted. The rating stays Low: individual students' outside-of-class habits may shift toward AI assistance, but the seminar's defining in-person, peer-dialogue structure is not substitutable by it.

At ten years, considerable uncertainty surrounds how career-transition guidance and peer mentorship are delivered across higher education generally, and AI advising tools will likely be markedly more capable and more embedded in students' independent preparation. Still, the specific instrumental activity Senior Seminar in Music provides — structured, live peer feedback and in-person conversation with music faculty and specialists about professional identity and next steps — is defined by real-time human presence rather than by a document or plan that could simply be generated. Nothing in the trajectory of generative AI substitutes for a room of graduating peers exchanging feedback face to face. The rating holds Low, with the caveat that the surrounding advising ecosystem a decade out may look quite different even as this course's embodied seminar format persists as the instrumental need.
MUS 4020.d: This course provides senior music majors with tools to navigate the next step. The work of the course is largely contained to class time, during which students provide peer review feedback, discuss relevant questions and materials, and meet with specialists in their areas. The course focuses on three questions: 1. What does it mean to be an educated musician in the 21st century? 2. What are the various sub-disciplines within the study and practice of music, and how do they overlap and interact in your own experience? 3. What is next? (Post-graduation plans and ideas)

r: Recital Preparation with the Collaborative Pianist develops the specific competence of rehearsing and performing in a duo with a professional pianist, the cornerstone instrumentation of Western art-music performance, culminating in a formal joint presentation. The instrumental work is live musical collaboration — balancing tempo, dynamics, and interpretation in real time with another performer — not a task reducible to a generated recording. Task-exposure research places embodied, real-time interpersonal performance activity well outside AI's automatable range, in contrast to writing and symbolic tasks it identifies as positively exposed. Verification of ensemble musicianship happens live, through the collaborative pianist's and applied-studio teacher's trained ear, with no adequate AI substitute for that judgment. At 24 months there is no erosion of the instrumental need; the rating is Low, grounded in embodiment.

By 2031, AI accompaniment and generative-audio tools will likely be far more capable at producing backing tracks or rehearsal aids, which could change how some students practice independently. But this course's instrumental purpose is specifically to develop rehearsal and performance skill with a live professional collaborative pianist under an applied-studio teacher's guidance, culminating in a formal joint recital — a real-time interpersonal partnership no synthetic accompaniment substitutes for. The jagged-frontier finding that AI users misjudge quality outside a model's true competence zone is a caution against treating machine-generated ensemble partnering as equivalent to trained human collaboration in performance contexts with real audiences. Embodiment and live verification both remain protective. The rating stays Low across the horizon; the course's function is inseparable from the human duo it trains.

A decade out, generative audio and interactive AI accompaniment systems will likely be considerably more sophisticated, and some rehearsal practice may increasingly involve AI-generated reference tracks. Even so, the instrumental task this course builds — collaborative, real-time musical judgment between a performer and a skilled human pianist, refined under faculty guidance toward a live formal recital — remains defined by embodied, in-person interaction that a model does not perform on the student's behalf. The honest uncertainty is how rehearsal tools evolve and whether collaborative-pianist roles themselves shift under industry pressure, not whether a student preparing for live recital performance still needs this trained human partnership. The rating holds Low, with embodiment and real-time verification continuing to anchor the course against any capability gains in generative audio.
MUS 4100.d: This course enables performers to develop rehearsal and performance practices under the guidance of a skilled professional collaborative pianist. The duo between pianist and orchestral instrumentalist or vocalist is the most common instrumentation in Western art music and represents a cornerstone of a performer's learning experience. The course culminates with formal presentations of the music prepared by the student and faculty pianist. The student and collaborative pianist will work in conjunction with applied studio teacher.

r: Analysis of Music applies traditional and modern analytical techniques to scores across forms and styles, producing written and notated analysis of harmonic, formal, and structural features. This is symbolic, text-and-notation-based work of the kind task-exposure research associates positively with AI exposure, distinct from the embodied performance courses elsewhere in the curriculum. Current models can already generate competent harmonic and formal analysis for clearly tonal repertoire, though nuanced interpretive judgment (voice-leading ambiguity, style-specific reasoning) still benefits from instructor verification. The course carries no general-studies designation and no licensure or accreditation clock-hour mandate, so no institutional lock protects it the way it protects gtPathways-designated theory-adjacent courses elsewhere. At 24 months, realized deployment of AI analytical tools in coursework is still emerging, keeping the rating at Medium rather than higher.

By 2031, capability-trend evidence pointing to rapidly lengthening AI task-time horizons suggests models will handle advanced score analysis — including more ambiguous structural and stylistic judgments — with substantially greater competence and at essentially no cost, and adoption of such tools in coursework is likely to be well underway. Because MUS 4110 carries no general-studies or accreditation designation, there is no institutional cap comparable to what constrains GT-Pathways survey courses; the rating is free to track task-level automatability directly. Verification burden is moderate rather than severe — a professor grading analytical work, not an adversarial or safety-critical context — so it does not depress the rating as strongly as it does in clinical or licensure-gated courses. The rating rises to High, reflecting genuine erosion of the instrumental need to perform this analytical labor unaided.

At ten years, uncertainty about exactly how sophisticated AI music analysis becomes is real, but the central-case trajectory in capability-trend research points toward AI handling most conventional and much advanced analytical work competently. With no gtPathways or accreditation designation anchoring MUS 4110 in the curriculum, nothing structurally protects the instrumental case the way institutional lock-in protects general-education theory courses. The course could plausibly persist for reasons outside this rating's scope — cultivating a musician's own analytical ear and vocabulary — but the specific task of producing advanced written analysis by hand is substantially automatable in the central case. The rating holds High, with the caveat that assessment design in analysis courses may shift toward evaluating AI-assisted or AI-generated analysis rather than eliminating analytical coursework outright.
MUS 4110.d: This course involves advanced analytical techniques applied to various music forms and styles. Traditional and modern methods of analysis are discussed.

r: Jazz Pedagogy transfers jazz performance skill into applied teaching knowledge by examining educational philosophies, objectives, and methods for teaching improvisation and jazz ensemble practice. Part of the work is conceptual and could draw on AI-generated summaries of pedagogical approaches, a textual task task-exposure research associates with positive exposure. But the applied core — modeling improvisational demonstration, live coaching of jazz performance technique, and real-time feedback on a student's playing — is embodied, in-person teaching activity that current AI systems do not perform. Verification of whether a teaching approach actually works requires a human instructor listening to live musical results, not evaluating a written plan alone. With no general-studies designation, the course is not institutionally locked; its Low rating instead reflects the embodied, real-time nature of jazz teaching demonstration itself.

By 2031, AI tools will likely generate increasingly sophisticated jazz pedagogy content — lesson sequences, practice frameworks, historical and stylistic context for improvisation instruction — accelerating the conceptual-preparation side of this course. Productivity research on professional writing tasks, where AI assistance cut time substantially while improving output quality, suggests similar gains could reach lesson-planning components of jazz pedagogy. The applied teaching demonstration itself, however, remains embodied: showing a student how to phrase a jazz line or comp behind a soloist in real time is not a task AI performs on the instructor's behalf. Because real-time interpersonal coaching stays central to what "teaching jazz" means, the dampening effect of embodiment continues to hold the rating at Low even as adjacent preparatory tasks become substantially AI-assisted.

A decade out, AI music tools will likely be deeply integrated into how aspiring jazz educators prepare materials, generate practice exercises, and study pedagogical literature, and the uncertainty is real about how much of that preparatory labor shifts to AI assistance. But the instrumental purpose of Jazz Pedagogy is training students to teach live improvisational performance to others, an activity built on embodied demonstration and real-time listening feedback that remains outside what generative AI substitutes for on a teacher's behalf. Even under a capability-forward scenario, an AI system does not stand in the room modeling a phrase or correcting a student's time feel. The rating holds Low, with the caveat concentrated on how much of the surrounding conceptual coursework becomes AI-assisted rather than on the embodied teaching core itself.
MUS 4350.d: This course expands and transfers jazz music performance skills into applied teaching knowledge by exploring educational philosophies, objectives, and methods.

r: Teaching Secondary Music I develops introductory competencies for teaching instrumental and vocal music at the secondary level, covering conceptual teaching, instructional strategies, classroom management, and assessment, and requires formal admission into the music education program with a corequisite 55-hour field placement (MUS 4361). The instrumental work is preparing students to manage and instruct real K-12 classrooms, an embodied, real-time interpersonal activity task-exposure research treats as low-exposure relative to solitary writing tasks. Colorado teacher-licensure programs require extensive field hours and a state-approved curriculum, and this course is a required methods component within that licensure-gated sequence, feeding directly into MUS 4370. Verification of teaching competence requires supervising faculty observing actual classroom conduct. The rating is Low, driven jointly by embodied classroom practice, licensure-program lock-in, and its foundational role for later required coursework.

By 2031, AI tools will likely be common for generating lesson plans, assessment rubrics, and classroom-management frameworks, and observed-usage data shows writing and planning tasks are already prominent in current AI use — some of that drafting labor in this course could plausibly shift toward AI assistance. But the course's instrumental core, methods training tightly coupled to a supervised field placement in real secondary classrooms, still requires embodied, in-person instructional practice and faculty verification of a candidate's classroom conduct that no model performs. Because the course sits inside a Colorado teacher-licensure curriculum with accreditation-linked field-hour requirements, institutional lock-in continues to cap the rating regardless of how automatable lesson-planning components become. The rating holds Low, with the licensure structure and embodied classroom-practice requirement both continuing to anchor it.

At ten years, AI-assisted lesson planning and instructional-content generation will likely be standard practice in teacher preparation broadly, and how music-education methods courses incorporate such tools is genuinely uncertain. What is more stable is that Colorado's teacher-licensure structure requires board-approved curricula with substantial field-experience components, and MUS 4360 remains a required course feeding directly into the paired field placement and the subsequent methods sequence. The core instrumental task — preparing a candidate to manage and instruct a live secondary classroom, verified through faculty observation of actual teaching — stays embodied and real-time regardless of how sophisticated AI planning tools become. The rating holds Low, with the licensure mandate and embodied classroom-practice requirement providing durable protection even as the broader teacher-prep landscape absorbs AI tools for preparatory work.
MUS 4360.d: Students develop introductory competencies for teaching instrumental music and technology at the elementary and secondary school levels. Course content includes experience with traditional vocal and instrumental teaching methodologies and their application to music teaching. Additional instruction includes conceptual teaching, instructional strategies, classroom management, assessment strategies, and the role of secondary music in education.

r: Supervised Field Experience in Secondary Music I places students in area secondary schools for a defined 55-hour supervised field experience, taken concurrently with MUS 4360, integrating methods coursework with direct classroom practice under a cooperating secondary music teacher. This is the clearest case of a hard, course-specific institutional mandate in this batch: the clock-hour requirement is fixed and central to Colorado's teacher-licensure pathway, comparable to clinical practicum structures in other licensure fields. The instrumental work is real-time, in-person instruction of actual secondary students, an embodied activity task-exposure research places well outside AI's automatable range, and its value is verified only through direct faculty and cooperating-teacher observation. At 24 months the rating is Low, anchored jointly by the embodied classroom presence requirement and the fixed clinical-hour licensure mandate.

By 2031, AI tools may assist secondary music teachers with lesson materials or assessment tracking in the schools where these placements occur, but that shift affects the cooperating teacher's workflow, not the instrumental requirement that a licensure candidate personally complete 55 hours of supervised, in-person field teaching. The clock-hour mandate is fixed by the licensure structure and does not shrink as adjacent tasks become AI-assisted; institutional brakes of this kind are explicitly slow-moving relative to capability growth. Embodiment remains the defining feature — a candidate must be physically present, managing a live classroom of secondary students, verified by direct observation — and no generative-AI capability substitutes for that presence. The rating holds Low, with the fixed clinical-hour requirement providing the more durable protection of the two anchoring factors.

A decade out, classroom technology and AI-assisted teaching tools will likely be far more embedded in secondary music education generally, but the licensure requirement this course fulfills — a defined block of supervised, in-person field teaching hours evaluated by direct observation — is an institutional structure that changes on a much slower timescale than AI capability itself, consistent with the general pattern that diffusion and regulatory adoption lag technical progress. The instrumental task remains a candidate's own embodied classroom presence and real-time instructional judgment with actual students, which is not a task performed on the candidate's behalf by any tool. The rating holds Low; the genuine uncertainty is how classroom practice looks technologically by 2036, not whether the clinical field-hour requirement and its embodied core persist.
MUS 4361.d: This course is designed to integrate concepts developed in MUS 4360 with practice in the classroom environment and must be taken concurrently with MUS 4360. Students work with secondary music teachers in area secondary schools in a fifty-five (55) hour supervised field experience.

r: Teaching Secondary Music II builds on MUS 4360 with advanced competencies for secondary music teaching, incorporating technology into instructional content while continuing to emphasize classroom management and assessment strategies, and pairs with a corequisite field placement (MUS 4371). This course sits inside the same Colorado teacher-licensure curriculum, requiring formal program admission and feeding a paired field experience with fixed clock-hour expectations. Verification of teaching competence continues to require direct faculty observation of actual instructional practice rather than review of a written product. The rating is Low, reflecting both the embodied classroom-practice core and the licensure-program's institutional lock-in.

By 2031, the technology-integration component this course explicitly covers will likely mean AI tools are a standard part of what candidates are taught to use in their own future classrooms, but that is a shift in course content, not in the instrumental need for the course itself. The advanced methods training and paired supervised field placement still require embodied, in-person teaching practice with real secondary students, verified through direct observation by supervising faculty and cooperating teachers. Because the course remains embedded in a licensure-gated curriculum with accreditation-linked field-hour structures, institutional lock-in continues to cap the rating regardless of how AI-assisted lesson preparation becomes. The rating holds Low, with embodiment and licensure structure both continuing to anchor it against erosion from adjacent AI capability.

At ten years, AI-assisted instructional technology will likely be thoroughly normalized in secondary classrooms, and this course's technology-integration content will have evolved considerably to reflect that reality — a genuine area of uncertainty in how the curriculum adapts. What remains comparatively stable is the licensure structure requiring a candidate to complete advanced methods training paired with supervised field teaching, verified through direct human observation of live classroom practice rather than through any generated artifact. The instrumental core — a candidate's own embodied capacity to manage and instruct a secondary classroom — is not a task AI performs on the candidate's behalf, regardless of how deeply AI tools are woven into the technology-integration curriculum they are taught to teach with. The rating holds Low across the horizon.
MUS 4370.d: Students develop advanced competencies for teaching secondary music at the secondary school levels. Course content expands on experiences with traditional music teaching methodologies, incorporating the use of technology as a means to facilitate musical content and concepts. Additional instruction includes classroom management, assessment strategies, and the role of secondary music in education.

r: This capstone course places students inside real secondary classrooms for a fifty-five-hour supervised field experience under practicing music teachers, integrating the concurrent methods content of MUS 4370 into live instructional practice. The work is classroom management, real-time pedagogical judgment, and mentor-observed teaching of actual adolescents, an in-person supervisory activity that task-exposure research places among the lowest-exposure categories because it depends on physical presence and moment-to-moment human responsiveness no model performs on the student-teacher's behalf. Colorado teacher-preparation programs carry field-hour requirements building toward roughly eight hundred secondary clock hours, and this course is a mandated component of that clinical sequence. By 2031, generative tools will likely assist candidates with lesson materials, differentiation strategies, and reflective journaling around their placements, but the course's core requirement is unchanged: physically present, mentor-evaluated teaching hours in a secondary music classroom. Verification of a candidate's classroom competence depends on a supervising teacher's direct observation, an embodied judgment AI cannot supply, and the Colorado field-hour mandate does not restructure within a single catalog cycle. The instrumental case stays anchored to licensure architecture rather than to how automatable individual planning tasks become. Augmentation may change what a candidate prepares beforehand, but it does not substitute for the fifty-five hours of supervised in-classroom practice the course exists to certify, so the rating holds at the floor across this horizon.

Even under a wide-uncertainty ten-year view in which classroom AI co-teaching assistants are commonplace, the field-experience requirement's function — certifying that a candidate can manage and teach real students under supervision — is not a task an AI performs for the student-teacher; it is embodied, evaluated professional practice students must complete themselves. The plausible decade-scale change is in what tools a candidate uses to prepare lesson materials, not in whether a licensure-track program still requires supervised clock hours inside an actual secondary classroom. Colorado's field-hour architecture could in principle be revised, which is the honest uncertainty here, but no evidence in hand suggests clinical practicum requirements for teacher licensure dissolve on this horizon. The rating remains Low, bound by licensure-gated embodied practice rather than by task automatability alone.
MUS 4371.d: This course is designed to integrate concepts developed in MUS 4370 with practice in the classroom environment and must be taken concurrently with MUS 4370. Students work with secondary music teachers in area secondary schools in a fifty-five (55) hour supervised field experience.

r: This course trains future piano teachers in methods, pedagogical literature, critical editions, and technique for private and group instruction, building on advanced applied study. What survives is the coaching competence itself — reading a student's playing in real time and adjusting instruction accordingly — which remains a verification-sensitive, embodied task; a mis-corrected technique has real, lasting cost to a developing pianist's physical habits. The productivity literature shows AI augmentation skewing toward drafting and synthesis rather than live interpersonal judgment, consistent with that split. Across a single catalog cycle the applied-teaching requirement is not restructured by improved literature tools. The rating stays Low: reference-material automation grows, but the embodied instructional practice the course exists to certify is not substituted.

A decade out, AI could plausibly generate sophisticated pedagogical repertoire recommendations, edition comparisons, and even technique explanations approaching expert quality, meaningfully eroding the course's knowledge-transmission function under a central-case trajectory. The programmatic contribution to teacher-training expectations tempers further erosion but does not fully offset it, since it is contributory rather than a hard course-specific mandate. The genuine uncertainty is how much course content shifts from literature mastery toward supervised coaching practice as institutions adapt; under the central case, meaningful task automation coexists with a residual embodied core.
MUS 4410.d: This course is a study of the methods, literature, editions, and techniques used in teaching piano privately and in groups.

Within a single catalog cycle the applied-teacher-training structure persists. The rating holds Low, anchored by the embodied diagnostic skill even as reference explanation becomes more automatable.

Over a decade, AI could plausibly deliver anatomically sophisticated, individualized guidance on vocal pedagogy and philosophy, substantially eroding the course's knowledge-transmission role in a wide-uncertainty central case. That shifts the rating to Medium: the explanatory content is meaningfully automatable, even though hands-on diagnostic listening and live correction for a young voice remain embodied and verification-sensitive enough to resist full substitution. The programmatic teacher-training contribution moderates but does not fully cap this erosion, since it is contributory rather than a hard course-specific mandate. The uncertainty is genuine — how much future coursework shifts toward supervised practicum as lecture content commoditizes — but under a central-case trajectory, meaningful automation of the explanatory core coexists with a residual coaching requirement AI does not replace.
MUS 4420.d: This course consists of a series of lectures, demonstrations, and discussions about physiology of the human voice (anatomy of the larynx, respiration, resonation, and articulation), young voices and how to teach them, and methods and philosophy of teaching voice.

r: This course surveys pedagogical methods and techniques for classical guitar across historical and recent approaches, alongside examination of canonical repertoire, preparing students to teach the instrument. The rating holds Low: reference material becomes more automatable while the supervised coaching practice the course is built to certify persists as the binding task.

A decade out, AI could plausibly generate sophisticated, individualized guitar-pedagogy curricula and repertoire recommendations, substantially eroding the course's knowledge-survey function under a wide-uncertainty central-case trajectory that assumes continued capability growth. The programmatic contribution to teacher-training expectations moderates the erosion without fully arresting it, since it is contributory rather than a hard course-specific mandate. The genuine uncertainty concerns how far supervised coaching practice displaces literature study as programs adapt to automatable reference content; the central case suggests meaningful task automation in the survey component alongside a residual embodied core the rating still credits.
MUS 4430.d: This course will survey a broad variety of pedagogical methods and techniques for the classical guitar, including both recent and historical approaches. In addition, the canonical repertoire for the classical guitar will be examined.

MUS 4440.d: This course enables students to develop performance skills and strategies for teaching instrumental and choral music in the areas of popular and jazz styles, as well as other electronic music practices.

Capability-trend research shows AI task horizons expanding quickly enough that multi-step planning and coordination tasks are a plausible target. Because roughly half the course's instrumental content is embodied, real-world event execution rather than digital planning, and no institutional lock-in protects it otherwise, the course likely sees rising but incomplete instrumental substitution, concentrated in its administrative and promotional tasks rather than its hands-on production requirement.
MUS 4882.d: This course examines how to plan, produce, promote, and manage special events, from small club gigs and fundraisers to festival concerts and publicity tours. Students start to build the organizational and communication skills necessary to design and execute such events. This course focuses on the analysis of past events, gaining insight into the processes and best practices for event creation and management. Additionally, students work to produce and/or manage original event(s) throughout the term.

r: This capstone-style course has students conduct extensive primary and secondary research on notable music-industry figures, managers, producers, executives, and artists, drawing out career lessons and models. The instrumental task is research synthesis and analytical writing, a fully digital activity with no live performance or in-person coordination component, placing it squarely among the task types task-exposure research identifies as strongly positively associated with AI exposure. AI research and writing assistants can already gather biographical and career information, synthesize patterns across multiple case subjects, and draft analytical narratives with reasonable competence, meaning a substantial share of this course's applied work is already achievable with current tools, even though a student's original synthesis and personal-application work still adds value. No general-studies designation or licensure structure offers institutional protection here.

At five years, AI research tools should be considerably better at synthesizing primary and secondary sources into coherent analytical case studies, and GDPval evidence showing models approaching human-expert parity on realized deliverables suggests this trajectory will continue toward research and writing outputs resembling this course's assignments. The verification burden stays moderate rather than high because factual accuracy in biographical research is checkable rather than adversarial, so no dampener applies, and the fully digital nature of the work means embodiment offers no protection either. With no accreditation or licensure floor, and a terminal, non-foundational role in the curriculum, the structural factors that protect other music courses do not apply here, pointing to a meaningfully reduced instrumental need for students to perform this research independently by this horizon.

Ten years out, generating well-sourced, well-synthesized case studies of industry figures and extracting career models from them is very plausibly within reach of AI systems at a high level of competence, continuing the trajectory already visible in research and writing tasks, though any point-prediction this far out carries real uncertainty. Capability-trend research shows AI task-completion horizons roughly doubling every several months, directly relevant to multi-source research synthesis of the kind this course requires. Because the task is fully digital, carries only moderate verification burden, and sits outside any institutional lock-in or foundational curricular role, this course's instrumental protection is among the weakest in the program, and continued erosion of the need for a human to manually perform this research is the more likely trajectory.
MUS 4884.d: This class critically assesses the careers of numerous notable figures in the modern music industry. This analysis of a cross section of managers, producers, record executives, artists and repertoire gurus, and publicity giants provides an intense, intimate, and in-depth insight into the lives and work of the industry's top professionals. Students are required to undertake extensive primary and secondary research on several notable music industry figures, drawing out lessons and developing models for their own careers.

r: This course covers song publishing workflows, copyright law across state, national, and international jurisdictions, publisher roles in acquisition, marketing, and creative development, standard deal terms, songwriting splits, negotiation strategy, registration, licensing, and synchronization -- primarily desk-based legal-analytical and writing work. Task-exposure research classifies programming and writing tasks as strongly positively associated with AI exposure, and contract-term summarization, royalty-split calculation, and copyright-basics explanation already fall within current model capability. At 24 months, though, students are still learning to read primary legal language, spot ambiguous split terms, and construct a workable negotiation position, skills instructors verify directly through applied assignments. No general-studies or licensure designation locks this course into the curriculum. The rating is Medium: contract-analysis and research tasks are exposed now, but the applied negotiation and legal-literacy competence the course builds is not yet reliably substituted without expert oversight of the details.

By 2031, AI drafting and negotiation-support tools will fluently summarize licensing agreements, flag unfavorable split terms, draft registration paperwork, and explain synchronization and licensing mechanics with much greater reliability than today. Observed-usage data already shows writing and knowledge-work tasks as a dominant share of AI use, and this course's core deliverables -- contract review, negotiation preparation, rights research -- sit squarely in that category. No general-studies mandate or licensure requirement anchors the course, so nothing but the course's own content protects it from erosion. The instrumental case weakens substantially: a student can increasingly lean on AI to interpret a publishing deal or draft licensing language competently. Verification burden is not negligible -- real money and rights are at stake -- but is not high enough to hold the rating down. Rating rises to High.

A decade out, under a central case of continued rapid capability growth, AI music-business assistants plausibly handle most routine publishing, licensing, and contract-negotiation-support tasks competently, and the capability-trend literature describes task-time-horizons for AI systems roughly doubling every four to seven months, compounding substantially by 2036. With no accreditation floor, licensure gate, or general-studies designation protecting this elective, and no embodiment involved, little structurally caps further erosion. The rating holds High, hedged: adoption still lags capability under diffusion research, and complex multi-party negotiations or novel legal disputes may retain a human-oversight premium the routine-task read does not capture. The course's instrumental case -- teaching students to do this work themselves -- is substantially weakened, even though understanding the underlying law and deal mechanics likely still matters for professionals directing AI-assisted negotiations.
MUS 4888.d: This course examines the processes of publishing songs, including the basics of how to navigate the complexities of state, national, and international copyright law. While reviewing a history of copyright law, students examine the roles of a publisher in acquisition, marketing, and creative development. The course also covers various types of publishing deals to familiarize students with their standard terms and conditions, as they learn to protect their rights as songwriters, artists, and managers. This course explores songwriting splits and how to negotiate a fair and equitable publishing deal. Students learn how to register their songs and examine the legalities of licensing and synchronization.

r: Senior Recital Performance is a live-performance capstone: students individually construct, organize, promote, and execute a public recital, rehearse repertoire spanning several contemporary genres, and write extensive program notes situating each selection historically, socially, and culturally. The central deliverable -- a live musical performance demonstrating technique, interpretation, and stage presence -- is embodied, real-time, and interpersonal, activities task-exposure research places outside AI's automatable range regardless of how capable generative audio becomes. Promotion and program-note writing carry some exposure, but they are peripheral to the graded core. Faculty mentors verify progress through in-person rehearsal review, a high-touch process no model performs on the student's behalf. No AI system currently substitutes for the act of preparing and delivering a live recital. Rating Low, driven by embodiment and verification, not by an absence of AI capability in adjacent tasks like promotional writing.

By 2031, AI tools will likely assist with recital promotion, program design, and even some drafting of program notes, and generative audio will be markedly more capable and prevalent in the broader music economy -- a market shift explicitly outside this rating's scope. The instrumental question is narrower: does the student still need to prepare and deliver the live performance themselves? The answer is unchanged. Embodiment and real-time interpersonal presence keep the graded core -- the recital itself -- non-substitutable, and faculty verification of live musicianship still requires a present human evaluator. Task-exposure research continues to place live performance activities among the least automatable. Peripheral administrative tasks erode further, but they are not what the course is graded on. The rating holds Low across a catalog cycle, with the caveat that the surrounding commercial-music labor market is considerably more exposed than this capstone's core requirement.

A decade out, under a wide-uncertainty central case, synthetic music and AI-generated promotional materials will likely be pervasive and highly capable. Even so, the specific competence this capstone certifies -- a student's ability to prepare, rehearse, and deliver a live musical performance in front of an audience and a faculty panel -- is not a task AI executes on the student's behalf; embodiment is definitional, not incidental. The most plausible ten-year change is in how much of the surrounding administrative and promotional work is AI-assisted, not in whether the live-performance requirement itself persists. The rating stays Low, hedged mainly by uncertainty about how recital assessment and promotion practices evolve rather than by any credible path to the live performance requirement itself being automated away by 2036.
MUS 4890.d: This course is the culmination of the student's degree in Commercial Music Performance. The student is responsible for individually constructing, organizing, promoting, and executing an individual recital. While they may perform with others, each musical selection must feature the student for which the degree is to be awarded. Students meet with their faculty mentor to discuss their ideas and progress toward their final performance. The individual student are required to organize rehearsals in preparation for the final performance. Students are also required to construct extensive program notes, which explain their choice of music, personnel and staging while situating each of their song selections within their proper historical, social, and cultural context. Students must display a high level of professionalism throughout the semester as well as within the final performance. Repertoire should include a mix of original and pre-existing material, which displays a wide range of performance skills in several contemporary music genres.

r: Students compile a portfolio of recordings and written scores, reflect critically on their own output to identify style, strengths, and gaps, devise a plan to round out a marketable collection, and produce a final performance of original songwriting work. Songwriting and composition are creative-generative tasks with real AI exposure -- generative music tools already draft melodies, chord progressions, and lyrics -- but assessing originality, personal voice, and portfolio coherence requires an instructor's trained ear, and the course culminates in a live performance of the student's own material. That embodied, verification-heavy combination keeps near-term erosion limited. No general-studies designation applies, though the course sits within the applied-study core NASM-oriented programs expect. At 24 months the instrumental need to personally write, refine, and perform original songs is essentially intact. Rating Low.

By 2031, generative songwriting tools will draft competent melodies, lyrics, and arrangements on demand, and observed-usage data already shows writing and creative-generation tasks as a large and growing share of AI use. The composition and recording-production side of the portfolio grows meaningfully more automatable. What continues to anchor the course is the final live performance requirement and the instructor's ongoing verification of authentic personal style and portfolio coherence -- judgments a human still makes about a human's own material. The applied-study contribution to the broader performance curriculum provides a partial, non-decisive hedge. On balance the rating holds Low rather than rising to Medium: the graded deliverable still requires the student's own compositional and performance labor, even as AI tools plausibly enter the drafting and production process as an aid rather than a replacement.

A decade out, generative composition tools will likely be capable of producing full, stylistically convincing songs with limited human input, substantially eroding the instrumental case for a student to originate musical and lyrical material unaided. The live-performance and originality-verification requirements provide a real but partial hedge -- an instructor must still confirm the work is the student's own -- rather than full protection. Under a wide ten-year uncertainty band, and absent any general-studies or licensure lock, the rating rises to Medium: composition tasks are substantially automatable, while the personal-performance and authenticity-verification core of the portfolio keeps the course from fully eroding. The honest caveat is that how songwriting pedagogy adapts to ubiquitous generative tools by 2036 is genuinely unsettled, and this projection carries real uncertainty.
MUS 4892.d: As a culmination of their studies, students compile an extensive and representative portfolio of their work to date, both recordings and written scores. Students examine and reflect on their own output as songwriters, identifying their style, strengths, weaknesses, and gaps in their resumes. Students devise and execute a plan to fill out their portfolio to establish a well-rounded and marketable collection of material, which allows them to take advantage of a wide range of opportunities in the contemporary music industry. Students are required to produce a final performance of their original songwriting work, which showcases their range of output to date.

r: This capstone has students conduct ethnographic and library/online research to identify potential career opportunities and demonstrate comprehensive understanding of the commercial-music field as it relates to those career paths -- a research-and-synthesis task with no performance or studio component of its own. Research retrieval, career-path analysis, and drafting synthesis documents sit among the more exposed knowledge-work activities; task-exposure research associates writing and analytical synthesis strongly and positively with AI exposure. There is no general-studies designation, licensure requirement, or embodiment protecting this course, and it is a terminal capstone with no later course depending on it. At 24 months, current tools already competently assist literature review and career-landscape summarization, though near-term classroom adoption and faculty verification of original synthesis still limit the realized effect. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI research assistants will competently synthesize labor-market and industry information, draft comparative career-path analyses, and structure findings into polished deliverables, and observed-usage data already shows research-and-writing tasks as a dominant category of AI use. With no institutional lock, foundational role, or embodiment constraint, little protects the course's research-and-synthesis core from broad automation. The instrumental case for a student personally conducting this research and writing it up erodes substantially -- AI can perform the retrieval, comparison, and drafting competently, leaving verification and personal career judgment as the residual human contribution. The rating rises to High, reflecting that the capstone's actual graded tasks are concentrated exactly where AI capability and adoption are advancing fastest, with the caveat that firm-level diffusion still lags capability under current adoption data.

A decade out, under a central case of continued rapid capability growth, AI systems plausibly perform the great majority of career-landscape research, comparative analysis, and written synthesis this capstone requires, with minimal human input needed for competent output. No accreditation floor, general-studies mandate, or embodiment requirement caps the erosion, and the course is terminal rather than foundational. The rating holds High, hedged by genuine ten-year uncertainty: capability trends point toward continued fast improvement, but how capstone assessment itself adapts -- shifting toward evaluating a student's judgment about AI-generated research rather than the research act itself -- is unresolved. The instrumental case for personally producing this research is substantially eroded even if the underlying career-exploration goal retains pedagogical purpose outside this rating's scope.
MUS 4899.d: This course is a culmination of the MSU @ DIME music degree, requiring students to integrate and apply the knowledge they have gained over the entirety of their studies. Students conduct ethnographic and library/online research in order to identify a range of potential career opportunities for themselves. Students demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of their field as they examine how these areas are relevant to their various potential career paths.

r: Techniques Practicum is advanced applied instruction on a student's primary instrument, developing professional-level technique through a logical progression of exercises across musical genres in preparation for the Commercial Music Capstone and Senior Recital. This is embodied, psychomotor skill-building -- real-time instructor feedback on tone, articulation, and physical execution -- the kind of activity task-exposure research consistently places outside AI's automatable range regardless of generative-audio progress. The course also sits directly in the applied-study prerequisite chain: it is required before Senior Recital Performance, giving it a moderate foundational role within the performance sequence. Verification of technical mastery happens through in-person lesson assessment a model cannot substitute for. At 24 months there is no meaningful erosion; the instrumental need is the student's own physical instrumental development. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI practice tools may offer feedback on rhythm, pitch accuracy, or repertoire suggestions, and the broader music-technology landscape will keep advancing, but that is a tooling question, not a substitute for the embodied technical development this practicum builds. The instrumental question remains whether a student still needs to physically develop instrumental technique through supervised practice, and the answer is unchanged: real-time psychomotor skill and live instructor verification are not tasks AI performs on the student's behalf. The course's position feeding directly into Senior Recital Performance continues to anchor it within the required applied-study sequence. Across a catalog cycle the technique-development requirement holds. The rating remains Low; AI may increasingly supplement practice sessions as a tool, but it does not replace the graded, embodied skill-acquisition process itself.

A decade out, even under a central case of highly capable AI music tools and pervasive synthetic audio, the specific competence this practicum develops -- a student's own physical mastery of their instrument at a professional technical level -- is not a task performed on the student's behalf by any model; the psychomotor learning process is intrinsically embodied. The prerequisite link to Senior Recital Performance keeps the course load-bearing within the applied-study sequence regardless of how the broader labor market for musicians evolves. The rating stays Low, with the caveat that ten years is a long horizon for surrounding technology and practice tools to change meaningfully, even if the instrumental requirement to personally build instrumental technique does not change nearly as much.
MUS 4910.d: This course is the culmination of technical development from the Techniques and Improvisation sequence. The course explores advanced technical concepts on a student's instrument in preparation for the Commercial Music Capstone Course and Senior Recital Performance. Students continue to learn professional-level techniques to further master the craft of their specific instrument, utilizing a logical progression of exercises and application. The course explores the technical vocabulary for a variety of musical concepts across numerous genres.

r: Personal Expression develops advanced improvisational concepts on a student's instrument, building a personal style through professional-level improvisation applied across varied musical contexts and genres, in preparation for the Commercial Music Capstone and Senior Recital. Improvisation is real-time, embodied musical decision-making performed live on an instrument -- task-exposure research places this kind of in-the-moment psychomotor and interpretive activity firmly outside AI's automatable range, distinct from AI's ability to generate recorded music offline. The course is a required prerequisite for Senior Recital Performance, anchoring it within the applied-study sequence rather than leaving it a free elective. Faculty verify improvisational competence through live, in-person assessment of a student's playing, a process no model can perform on the learner's behalf. At 24 months the instrumental need for personal, embodied improvisational development is unchanged. Rating Low.

By 2031, generative-audio systems will produce increasingly convincing improvisation-style music offline, and that will matter for the broader creative-music economy -- a market question this rating explicitly excludes. The narrower instrumental question is whether a performance student still needs to personally develop live improvisational fluency on their instrument, and the answer holds: real-time musical decision-making in performance is not a task a model executes for the student, and verification depends on an instructor hearing the student play live. The prerequisite relationship to Senior Recital Performance continues to keep this course structurally necessary within the sequence. Across a catalog cycle the requirement to build this specific embodied skill is unchanged. The rating remains Low, with the caveat that AI-generated music increasingly reshapes what improvisational competence is valued for professionally after graduation.

A decade out, under a wide-uncertainty central case, AI-generated improvisational-style audio will likely be sophisticated and widespread, but the course's actual instrumental need -- a student's own capacity to improvise live, in real time, in front of listeners -- is not something a generative model performs on the student's behalf; embodiment and real-time presence are the substance of the skill being taught, not incidental features of it. The prerequisite chain into Senior Recital Performance keeps the course load-bearing within the required sequence regardless of shifts in the surrounding creative-music labor market. The rating stays Low, hedged mainly by uncertainty over how practice and pedagogy evolve around AI tools, not by any plausible path to live improvisational skill-building itself being automated away.
MUS 4920.d: This course represents the culmination of improvisation and self-expression skills learned from the Techniques and Improvisation sequence. The course explores advanced improvisational concepts on a student's instrument in preparation for the Commercial Music Capstone Course and Senior Recital Performance. Students continue to experiment with professional-level improvisational concepts to further develop their personal style of expression on their instrument. Students apply their improvisational skills within a variety of musical contexts across numerous genres.

r: Senior Project lets students pursue an in-depth project in theory, history, literature, education, composition, performance practice, pedagogy, or music therapy, culminating in a scholarly written document and, if not research-based, additional evidence such as performance or a web-based product. The constant requirement -- a scholarly, well-documented written work -- carries real research and drafting exposure, but disciplinary depth, originality, and adherence to departmental documentation standards require sustained instructor verification across a semester. This flexibility means task exposure varies by topic: composition or performance-based projects lean embodied and creative, while historical or pedagogical projects lean toward exposed research-writing tasks. There is no general-studies designation on this course, but it fulfills the BA in Music's Senior Experience requirement, a program-level rather than GT-Pathways mandate. At 24 months the instrumental need for the student's own scholarly work is largely intact. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI research and writing tools will competently draft literature reviews, structure scholarly documents, and even assist with music-historical or theoretical analysis, materially eroding the writing-heavy end of this flexible project's task mix. Composition- and performance-based projects retain more embodied, less-automatable content, but the written-document requirement applies to every student regardless of topic, and that shared core is increasingly exposed. Sustained instructor verification of originality and documentation quality across a full-semester project remains a meaningful check, keeping the erosion partial rather than complete. No general-studies mandate protects the course, only its own project-verification structure and, for some topics, embodied deliverables. The rating holds Low: the mandatory written-document component grows more automatable, but close faculty oversight of a self-directed capstone keeps the instrumental case from clearly shifting upward yet.

A decade out, AI systems plausibly perform sophisticated scholarly research, analysis, and drafting across most of this project's possible topics, and the capability-trend literature describes AI task-time-horizons compounding rapidly over a decade. For topics without an embodied performance or composition component, the instrumental case for a student personally producing the scholarly document weakens substantially. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting that variance: performance- and composition-based Senior Projects retain a meaningfully protected embodied core, while research-and-writing-heavy projects erode further, and the aggregate course-level rating sits between those extremes. The honest hedge is that how the department restructures Senior Project requirements and assessment as AI writing tools mature is genuinely uncertain, and the flexible topic structure makes one precise ten-year prediction less reliable than for a narrower, single-track course.
MUS 4950.d: In this course, the student prepares an in-depth and focused project related to music theory, music history, music literature, music education, composition, performance practice, pedagogy, music therapy, or other music-specific topics. Students complete a project that may be research-based or result in a creative body of work, but includes a research component and a written document. If the project is not research-based, other evidence of work will be included in addition to the written document, such as performance, web-based product, or other significant work approved by the instructor. The written document created by the student shall be scholarly and well documented according to departmental standards. Fulfills the Senior Experience requirement for the BA in Music.

r: This capstone has students compose original music, oversee public performances of their compositions, and deliver a public lecture on their own compositional activities -- a sequence combining creative-generative work with live performance oversight and real-time public speaking. Composition itself carries real AI exposure through generative-music tools, but overseeing a live public performance and delivering an in-person lecture on one's own creative process are embodied, interpersonal activities task-exposure research keeps outside the automatable range. Faculty verify compositional originality and the quality of live performance oversight directly, a high-touch process. The course sits within the applied-study and composition core NASM-oriented programs expect, giving it partial institutional grounding short of a full mandate. At 24 months, the instrumental need for the student's own composition, oversight, and public presentation is essentially intact. Rating Low.

By 2031, generative-composition tools will draft increasingly sophisticated original music, and observed-usage data shows creative-writing and generation tasks as a substantial and growing share of AI use, meaningfully eroding the compositional-drafting side of this project. What continues to anchor the course is overseeing an actual live public performance of the work and delivering a real-time public lecture -- both embodied, interpersonal activities a model does not perform on the student's behalf, and both directly verified by faculty and audience. The applied-study contribution provides a partial hedge. On balance the rating holds Low: composition drafting grows more automatable, but the graded capstone experience is inseparable from live performance oversight and public presentation, which keep the course's core requirement largely intact across a catalog cycle.

A decade out, generative-composition systems will likely produce highly convincing original music with limited human authorship, substantially eroding the instrumental case for a student to compose unaided. The live-performance-oversight and public-lecture components provide a real but partial hedge -- someone must still organize, direct, and speak to a live audience about the work, coordinating musicians and staging -- rather than full protection, since composition is the project's namesake task. Under a wide ten-year uncertainty band, and with only partial institutional grounding, the rating rises to Medium: the compositional-authorship core is meaningfully automatable while the embodied performance-oversight and public-presentation components resist substitution. How composition pedagogy and capstone assessment adapt to mature generative-music tools by 2036 remains genuinely unsettled and hard to pin down with any real precision.
MUS 4960.d: This is the final composition project in which students compose, oversee public performances of their compositions, and give a public lecture on their compositional activities.

r: This is a supervised, full-time eight-week student-teaching placement in an accredited elementary school, giving teacher-candidates increasing responsibility for instructing, supervising, and assessing K-6 learners, backed by university-supervisor observations and five hours of seminar. The applied work -- real-time classroom instruction, behavior management, formative assessment of young children -- is embodied, interpersonal, and psychomotor, activities task-exposure research places well outside AI's automatable range even as lesson-planning and grading-support tools grow more capable. The binding constraint is licensure: candidates must be rated proficient against Colorado Teacher Quality Standards to receive MSU Denver's recommendation for licensure, a hard course-specific mandate with required clinical clock hours that a state board, not a curriculum committee, controls. F4=1 caps the rating at Low regardless of how automatable adjacent administrative tasks become. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI tools will likely be common in lesson planning, differentiated-materials generation, and administrative documentation for teachers, but the licensure structure this course serves is unchanged: Colorado's teacher-quality standards and the clinical-placement requirement remain a board-controlled mandate independent of classroom-technology diffusion. The instrumental question is whether a candidate still needs supervised, in-person clinical teaching experience to earn a licensure recommendation, and institutionally the answer is yes -- this is precisely the kind of hard, course-specific lock the framework treats as capping erosion regardless of task automatability. Real-time instruction and in-person assessment of a candidate's classroom performance also remain embodied and verification-heavy. The rating holds Low, anchored by licensure rather than by an absence of AI capability in the surrounding teaching profession.

A decade out, under a wide-uncertainty central case, AI will likely handle much of the administrative and lesson-preparation burden surrounding K-6 teaching, and the profession itself may be reshaped by classroom AI tools in ways hard to fully anticipate today. But absent a change to Colorado licensure statute or Board-approved program structure, the clinical student-teaching requirement this course represents persists as a hard institutional lock, and the embodied, real-time work of instructing, supervising, and managing a classroom of children remains outside what a model performs on the candidate's behalf. The rating stays Low. The genuine uncertainty is how classroom practice and teacher-preparation curricula evolve around AI tools over a decade, not whether the licensure-gated clinical placement itself remains required for certification.
MUS 4971.d: This is a supervised, full-time, eight week student teaching experience in an accredited public or private elementary school, providing increasing responsibility for the teaching, supervision, and assessment of learners (grades K-6). Regularly scheduled observations and five hours of seminars conducted by an appointed university supervisor are part of the student teaching requirement. Teacher-candidates must complete a teacher work sample and be rated as proficient in all Colorado Teacher Quality Standards to receive MSU Denver's recommendation for teacher licensure.
